articles.title: British and French troops war-game attack on NATO territory
articles.body:
British and French troops war-game attack on NATO territory
- British and French troops joined the Rhino Titan exercise in Germany to test NATO defence against a modern attack, including drones and electronic warfare.
- About 2,500 troops took part over seven weeks, with 600 paratroopers dropping from four RAF A400M Atlas aircraft in one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in 20 years.
- The drill comes amid fears of Russian aggression in Europe, and Wes Streeting said it shows NATO can deliver rapid airborne power to defend territory and deter adversaries.
AI generated
LONDON – Thousands of British and French troops have taken part in a military training exercise that included one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in two decades, the British government said on Oct 25.
The war game is designed to show how NATO countries could be defended against a modern-day attack and comes during fears about Russian aggression in Europe amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Some 2,500 troops were involved in the seven-week exercise, in which 600 British and French paratroopers dropped from four RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft over Germany.
The exercise, called Rhino Titan and held at the Sennelager military training centre in Germany, has been testing British troops’ ability against an enemy equipped with drones and electronic warfare.
“The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly,” British Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.
“Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend NATO territory.
“This combination of troops and specialised equipment is what is required to deter adversaries and keep Britain and our allies safe,” he added.
In recent years, Western nations have accused Russia of waging a “hybrid” campaign of espionage, sabotage, including damage to subsea cables, and other disruptions – charges that Moscow has vehemently denied. AFP

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia launches 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine in one week
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia launches 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine in one week
President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
“This week alone, Russia has fired approximately 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types—including ballistic missiles—and nearly 2,300 attack drones at Ukraine. Unfortunately, there are casualties and injuries from these brutal strikes almost every day,” Zelensky said.
He noted that four people were killed and 22 others were wounded—including an 11-year-old girl—as a result of Russian shelling in the Dnipropetrovsk region that evening. In Vinnytsia, a Russian drone struck a high-rise building, wounding six people. In Kharkiv, the Russians first struck a construction supply store and then cynically launched a second strike against the emergency services that had arrived at the scene. Rescue workers were injured. “There were also strikes last night on thermal power plants, substations, coal mines, grain silos, shopping centers, and a postal terminal. There is damage in nine regions,” the President noted.
He emphasized that this is precisely how Russia responds to diplomacy and efforts to end its isolation, and it is very important that support for pro-life advocates not wane alongside the negotiation track.
“We need to unblock the delivery of interceptors for the ‘Patriots,’ which has already been agreed upon by the Europeans. We need to continue supporting Ukraine’s combat aviation to defend against ‘Shahed’ drones. Every such defense package, especially ahead of winter, helps save lives,” the head of state noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky stated that the Russians will intensify their ballistic attacks against Ukraine, especially as supplies of interceptor missiles to Ukraine decrease.

articles.title: What to know about Melania Trump’s Oleshky ceasefire deal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, is set to get a brief pause in the 4 1/2-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
US First Lady Melania Trump brokered the localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city she said is "on the brink of disaster."
Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but they have not released many details.
Oleshky has been without power, heat or water
Oleshky is located in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. Moscow's forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organise evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Ceasefire, aid, then evacuations
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, then humanitarian aid delivery, then the evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman and chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, Lubinets said, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city.
Russia's human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
The pause begins Tuesday and will last several days
Lubinets told the AP that the ceasefire will begin Tuesday, two days before the humanitarian mission starts, and will last several days.
Russia's chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces "will cease fire on the Kherson axis" from 4 AM Tuesday Moscow time, which is late Monday in the United States. He said Russian forces would also carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and ensure the "humanitarian convoy" can move safely into the city.
Ukraine's General Staff said the ceasefire will begin at 3 AM Tuesday Kyiv time, since Ukraine moves its clocks back an hour on Sunday while Russia does not.
Lubinets said the pause would apply across the Kherson region and neighbouring areas essential to the operation.
Key details have not been released 
Lubinets gave no details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or carried out, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said people who want to leave Oleshky can do so. He would not say whether they would be taken to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory. Asked how long the evacuation would last, he said only that it would most likely take several days.
"The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement," Lubinets said.
The first lady took up the issue at the UN
The first lady began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the UN General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
"When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination," Lubinets said. He said the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing "new approaches, mechanisms and tools" to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband's second term. She hosted a UN Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
Last year she wrote to Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as "displaced by the war." Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, says she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine's government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with President Donald Trump and other top US officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, agreed with Russia to import diesel fuel, and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the Oleshky ceasefire during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank, on Friday. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold.
He also stressed the importance of the United States in renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant more than 1,400 kilometers from border, monitoring channel claims
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant more than 1,400 kilometers from border, monitoring channel claims
Ukrainian forces struck Avisma, one of the world's largest titanium sponge producers, in Berezniki, Perm Krai, on Oct. 25, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said at around 11 a.m. local time that 11 drones had been downed during a Ukrainian attack on the region.
Makhonin added that an "industrial facility" in the northern part of the region had sustained "minor" damage but continued to operate as normal. The governor did not specify which facility had been damaged.
According to Makhonin, five employees of the facility were also injured in the Ukrainian attack.
Exilenova+ said the strike targeted Avisma, located about 170 kilometers (105 miles) from the city of Perm. The plant is part of Russian metallurgical corporation VSMPO-AVISMA.
Located more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border, Avisma has been under U.S. sanctions since 2023. The plant manufactures products used in military aircraft, nuclear submarines, armored vehicles, and missile systems.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine's General Staff said Ukrainian forces also struck Russian military radar stations in Belgorod Oblast overnight on Oct. 25, as well as a Russian command post in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command-and-observation post in occupied Kherson Oblast.
Other targets included concentrations of Russian troops in the occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, the General Staff added.
Earlier, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk following a Ukrainian attack.
The overnight attack on Belgorod also damaged a local shopping and entertainment center, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Belgorod Mayor Valentin Demidov said one person was killed and 10 others were injured in the attack. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged, he added.

articles.title: Netanyahu posts image of atomic bomb over Tel Aviv: ‘Nothing else will matter’
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday shared an AI-generated image depicting an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv, accompanied by a stark warning about Iran's nuclear ambitions, just two days before Israelis head to the polls. The post, which suggested that domestic political controversies pale in comparison with the threat from Tehran, drew a sharp response from Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, who accused Netanyahu of spreading panic.
Alongside the image, Netanyahu quoted Yuval Bloomberg, an Israeli writer and political commentator best known for his book The Oslo Trap, which critically examines the 1993 Oslo Accords and their consequences for Israeli security.
"The State of Israel faces a real and tangible existential threat," Bloomberg wrote. "If the Iranians obtain nuclear weapons, nothing else will matter anymore. Everything is so trivial compared with the existential danger posed by Iran and the Shiite axis."
The post also repeated the argument that Israel has only two more years under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to address the Iranian threat, portraying disputes dominating Israeli politics as distractions from the country's most pressing security challenge.
"Qatar, the ultra-Orthodox, Urich, military conscription, warnings. It's all one giant smokescreen designed to conceal the one issue that towers above everything else," the post read. "If two atomic bombs fall on central Israel, who will care about all these meaningless controversies?"
The image and accompanying message came as Israel entered the final stretch of its election campaign, with voters set to cast their ballots Tuesday, October 27. Netanyahu has emphasized the threat from Iran throughout the campaign, arguing that confronting Tehran's nuclear ambitions must remain Israel's overriding national priority.
Golan, a former IDF deputy chief of staff and chairman of the Democrats party, condemned the post and accused the prime minister of attempting to frighten voters.
"The prime minister of Israel has posted an image of an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv," Golan said. "I ask that he be kept away from social media. The man and those around him have lost it. The pressure is mounting."
Golan also linked his criticism directly to the upcoming election, saying: "On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and sanity to Israel."

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Musk of false claims over Starlink
articles.body:
- Ukraine rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military used civilian Starlink for offensive drone strikes in breach of SpaceX’s terms of service.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Starlink terminals in Ukraine have been capped at 70-90 km/h since February 2026 and do not work over Russia.
Ukraine has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military broke Starlink’s terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes, with a presidential adviser saying that restrictions SpaceX placed on the service in February make such use physically impossible.
Musk made the accusation on X on Oct. 24, the same day Ukraine said its satellite access had been restored after more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted front-line operations.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” wrote SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
In the same post, Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version of the network, “is controlled by the US government,” and that Starlink remains critical to Ukraine’s defense because it is “the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now.” He wrote that Ukraine’s front line “would collapse immediately” if Starlink were turned off, said SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth, and closed by telling people he called warmongers, “May you burn in hell.”
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology, responded that Musk’s claim ignores how Starlink actually works in Ukraine. Since February 2026, he said, every Starlink terminal over Ukrainian territory, including occupied areas, has been capped at movement speeds of 70 to 90 km/h (43 to 56 mph), and Starlink does not work over Russia at all.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” said Beskrestnov. “Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and middle strikes.”
A terminal capped at road speeds cannot stay connected aboard an attack drone, and the long-range strikes Musk referred to take place over Russian territory, where the service is switched off.
Serhii Sternenko, who worked on the issue at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense as an adviser to Mykhailo Fedorov, said the system Ukraine built in February left no room for the misuse Musk described. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians, but any terminal used on the move had to be placed on a special list and connected to Starshield.
“In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield,” wrote Sternenko.
“We are very grateful to the United States and SpaceX for access to critically important satellite communications. Ukraine did not violate the terms of use,” wrote Sternenko.
Musk’s Oct. 24 post differs from what he said 10 days earlier. On Oct. 14, as speed limits disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, Mykhailo Fedorov wrote on X that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h (99 mph) was being restored and that removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely had become critical for Ukraine’s defense. Musk replied the same day that the limits were not SpaceX’s decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” wrote Musk on Oct. 14. “Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
President Donald Trump has said he did not order the restrictions. CBS News and The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week that Musk was behind the slowdown, and his Oct. 24 post was the first time he said SpaceX had closed what he called a loophole.
Ukrainian commanders said the restrictions cost them drones and disrupted missions. Starshield has become the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and battlefield communications, including the interceptor drones used against Russian attack drones. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that full use had been restored, with its monitoring systems recording stable connections on objects moving faster than 400 km/h (250 mph).

articles.title: Zelenskyy reports damage caused by latest Russian attacks
articles.body:
Zelenskyy reports damage caused by latest Russian attacks
Russian forces attacked a thermal power plant, substations, coal mines, grain storage facilities, shopping centres and a postal logistics hub on the night of 24-25 October.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Details: This week alone, Russia has launched around 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, almost every day, these brutal strikes leave people killed and injured," Zelenskyy said.
Four people were killed in Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the evening of 24 October. Another 22 people were injured, including an 11-year-old girl.
In Vinnytsia, a Russian drone struck an apartment building, injuring six people.
In Kharkiv, Russian forces first struck a home improvement superstore and then carried out a repeat strike on emergency services that had arrived at the scene. Rescue workers were injured.
Quote: "There were also strikes overnight on a thermal power plant, substations, coal mines, grain storage facilities, shopping malls and a postal logistics hub. Damage has been reported in nine regions. [...]
We need to unblock the deliveries of Patriot interceptors already approved by European countries. We need to continue supporting Ukrainian combat aviation to defend against jet-powered Shaheds. Every such defence package, especially ahead of winter, helps save lives."
Background:
- An outage caused by an emergency has left parts of the Holosiivskyi, Solomianskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts of Kyiv without electricity.
- An energy facility was struck in Vinnytsia Oblast, triggering emergency power cuts in one district of the oblast.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles, drones as fighting with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis continues
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over its capital, Riyadh, and southern areas on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, as fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists persisted.
The conflict has become an increasingly destabilizing front following the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
On Sunday, Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait, before announcing minutes later that the danger had passed.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted ten ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis warned they could again target Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after a deadly attack earlier this month.
Houthis claim responsibility for attacks on Saudi airport, oil facilities
The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and warned all airlines, airport staffers and travelers against using it.
Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.
The airport halted operations on October 10 following an attack - claimed by the Houthis - that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on Bab el-Mandeb Strait - a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, a year earlier.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles and drones as fighting with Houthis rages
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles and drones as fighting with Houthis rages
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted drone and missile launched towards Riyadh and 10 missiles targeting the southern region.
Saudi Arabia has intercepted drones and missiles over its capital, Riyadh, and southern areas, the Saudi-led coalition has said, as fighting with Yemen’s Houthis continues.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on Sunday its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the capital city that morning, as well as a drone in the Riyadh region, and a cruise missile aimed at the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, with explosions ringing out in the Saudi capital.
It later reported the interception of 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The attacks come as operations resumed at two terminals at Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid international airport after deadly attacks earlier this month by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
Operations at the airport were halted on October 10 after 13 people were killed and more than 300 others were wounded in a Houthi attack.
Late on Saturday, Riyadh airport said in a statement that international flights would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target” for the Iran-backed group.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.”
The Iran-aligned Houthis on Saturday said they targeted three Saudi airports, including one in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an airbase.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting Mecca and Medina, two of the holiest cities in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.
In Yemen on Sunday, the Houthis advanced on Jabal Sabr, the strategic mountain overlooking the city of Taiz, which has become the focus of the fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s government forces.
Houthi fighters have besieged the city and cut off the main road to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The United Nations has warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped in the city.
Yemen’s government forces, meanwhile, said they conducted more than 700 operations against Houthi targets on Saturday, claiming to have killed more than 300 fighters.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen in recent weeks, causing a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
The war in Yemen escalated sharply when the Houthis seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a huge blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and normal life, and damaging its international image.

articles.title: The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
articles.body:
The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
TEHRAN - The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has exposed the limits of American military power and the dangers of an administration that appears to have mistaken technological superiority for the ability to dictate political outcomes, William H. McRaven, who served in the U.S. Navy, wrote in Foreign Affairs.
Launched on February 28 without a clearly defined rationale or attainable objectives, the war illustrates Washington’s persistent failure to learn from the costly experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq.
From the outset, the Trump administration’s objectives have been inconsistent. Initially, Washington spoke of regime change and eliminating Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Later, reopening the Strait of Hormuz became a central priority, even though the waterway had not been closed before the war began. Trump’s contradictory statements about these objectives have raised serious questions about whether his administration had a coherent strategy or adequately considered the consequences of military action.
“The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives—from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East,” McRaven stated.
At the heart of this failure lies an enduring American illusion: that overwhelming military superiority can overcome political, geographical, and strategic realities. Advanced aircraft, precision weapons, and sophisticated intelligence systems can inflict enormous damage, but they cannot automatically force a determined adversary to surrender or produce the political changes Washington desires. Iran’s geography, its capacity to challenge shipping through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, and its determination to resist foreign aggression all place significant limits on the effectiveness of American military power.
The administration’s approach has also undermined its international standing. According to the analysis, Washington launched the war without first building international legitimacy or consulting its allies, including neighboring Arab states. Its failure to acknowledge responsibility for an airstrike that reportedly killed 120 students at an Iranian elementary school further damaged its moral credibility. When Trump subsequently sought international assistance to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the administration encountered resistance from countries whose support it had failed to cultivate.
Such miscalculations reflect a broader problem in American policymaking: the growing concentration of presidential power and the politicization of institutions responsible for providing independent military, diplomatic, and intelligence advice. When personal loyalty takes precedence over professional judgment, warnings about the costs and risks of war may be ignored. The result can be a dangerous cycle in which overconfidence produces reckless decisions, and those decisions generate consequences that military force alone cannot reverse.
The experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq should have taught Washington that wars without clear objectives, broad international support, and realistic exit strategies can become prolonged strategic failures. Yet the Trump administration appears to have repeated these mistakes, underestimating both Iran’s capacity to resist and the broader regional consequences of attacking it.
Ultimately, the war underscores a fundamental truth: military supremacy does not amount to unlimited political power. Geography, national resistance, international legitimacy, and the quality of leadership remain decisive factors in determining the outcome of conflicts. The central lesson is clear: no amount of firepower can compensate for a reckless strategy, contradictory objectives, and a failure to understand the adversary.

articles.title: Musk says Ukrainian military violated Starlink terms of use, loophole has been closed
articles.body:
Musk says Ukrainian military violated Starlink terms of use, loophole has been closed
US billionaire and SpaceX owner Elon Musk has commented on restrictions on access to Starlink, claiming that the Ukrainian military had violated the terms of use for this type of communications system. He also said that if Starlink were switched off, "the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
Source: Musk on X (Twitter)
Quote: "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be… Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
Details: Musk said that Starshield is a separate system controlled by the US government. "What they decide to do is up to them," he wrote.
"Starlink remains critical to the defence of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
In his view, Starlink was also crucial in preventing Russia from occupying Ukraine in the early stages of the war, as Russia had destroyed or jammed all other means of communication.
Quote: "SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR. That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signalling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell."
Details: Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that restrictions on Starlink and Starshield had been lifted as of the morning of 24 October and thanked everyone who had helped restore communications in Ukraine.
Previously:
- On 21 October, after reports of the speed reduction became public, Musk wrote: "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
- Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had ordered the speed of the military version of Starlink to be reduced in Ukraine, leaving some Ukrainian attack and interceptor drones practically unusable.
- On 22 October, the WSJ reported that US President Donald Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
Background:
- On 19 October, Zelenskyy said that Starlink and Starshield equipment had stopped working at speeds of 130-161 km/h in various sectors of the line of contact, disrupting logistics and limiting Ukraine's use of drones.
- On 16 October, Trump claimed that the White House had not been involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system.
- Meanwhile, The Telegraph reported that Musk had approached Trump with the idea of restricting the bandwidth of the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military.

articles.title: 'Don't film missiles': India advises its nationals in Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi strikes
articles.body:
Indian embassy has urged its nationals in Saudi Arabia not to film or share information about missile and drone interceptions, warning of legal consequences amid ongoing regional tensions
NEW DELHI: India on Sunday advised its nationals in Saudi Arabia to follow local rules and refrain from filming or sharing information about missile and drone interceptions, amid ongoing attacks linked to Yemen’s Houthis.“The Indian community residing in Saudi Arabia is requested to abide by local rules and regulations,” the embassy said on social media while reposting a notification issued by the directorate of Saudi civil defence.
“Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability,” the notification said.The embassy also shared an update on flight disruptions, saying Air India and Air India Express services to and from Riyadh and Dammam would remain suspended until November 7, while flights to and from Jeddah would remain suspended until October 31.The consulate general of India in Jeddah said its 24x7 control rooms in Jeddah and Makkah continued to assist affected Indians with food, essential medicines and other immediate requirements, wherever feasible.
The consulate added that it was in regular contact with Saudi Arabia’s ministry of Hajj and Umrah and ministry of foreign affairs to address difficulties caused by the flight disruptions, particularly those involving visa validity and delayed departures.
Meanwhile, Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport was preparing to resume domestic and international flight operations on Sunday, Gulf News reported.The report also cited the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis as saying that air defences had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh on Sunday.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

articles.title: American are done paying for Trump’s family business
articles.body:
American are done paying for Trump’s family business
TEHRAN — Donald Trump won the White House promising to “Make America Great Again,” then promised Americans a short, cheap war on Iran. They got a closed Strait of Hormuz, Brent crude above $116 a barrel, and gasoline past $5 a gallon in several states. He and his family got a windfall.
Nine days before the November 3 midterms, the distance between those two experiences has become the central fact of American politics.
In CNBC’s final pre-election survey, 36 percent of registered voters named government corruption among their top issues, ahead of food prices at 34 percent and gasoline at 23 percent.
Fox News found 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. People are reading their grocery receipts and the headlines as one story.
A war with a customer list
The campaign of aggression against Iran has already cost tens of billions of dollars, paid from the public purse. Some of it is landing with companies the president’s sons own or advise.
Powerus, which Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are backing toward a stock listing, holds an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million for interceptors meant to counter Iranian drones.
Skeptics doubt the systems can stop Iran’s one-way attack drones, which have proved themselves in large numbers. Powerus is pitching them to Arab governments in the Persian Gulf anyway, the same clients Washington claims to be defending.
Trump Jr. also holds roughly $4 million in Unusual Machines, where he serves as an adviser. The “War” Department bought 3,500 drone motors and related parts from the company, and the Army has floated a follow-on order of 20,000.
Its shares jumped when his link became public. Rep. Jason Crow says firms tied to the sons have drawn about $3.7 billion in federal money this term.
The youngest Trump son, Barron, joined 1789 Capital days after the 2024 election. Among its holdings is Anduril, approved for a possible $2 billion interceptor sale to Kuwait.
Trump’s own portfolio includes Palantir, Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman, whose revenues have swelled with U.S. military warmongering.
Richard Painter, who served as ethics lawyer in George W. Bush’s White House, told the Wall Street Journal that he sees no modern precedent. That is a notable benchmark, given the Bush administration’s own notorious record of foreign aggression and corporate enrichment.
Persian Gulf states, he says, are “under immense pressure to buy from Trump’s sons,” so the president will deliver what they want. It may be the first time, he adds, that a president’s family has made vast sums from a war launched without congressional authorization.
Arab monarchy money and a crypto pipeline
The Persian Gulf runs through the family’s earlier business too. In his upcoming book Princes and Thieves, Matthew Cole reports that Jared Kushner had access to at least two accounts tied to the UAE and Israel, together receiving about $2 billion, part of it Saudi-backed and moved through banks in Baku.
Dutch intelligence, which had penetrated his phone, helped trace the transfers. A third account, the report says, paid for an Israeli pledge to defend the Emirates against Iranian strikes.
Then came crypto. Days before the 2025 inauguration, an entity backed by Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million.
An Abu Dhabi fund he chairs later bought $2 billion of the firm’s USD1 stablecoin. Months on, the administration eased AI chip exports to Emirati firms, including G42, which Tahnoon controls.
Trump also pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company had paid $4.3 billion in fines, and accepted a $400 million jet from Qatar.
On October 22, a Circle shareholder sued in federal court, alleging violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.
Trump’s disclosures show $2.2 billion in earnings for his first year back, $1.4 billion of it from crypto, including about $636 million from a memecoin whose promoters advertised a dinner with him for its 185 biggest holders.
‘Slime, not crime’
Smaller scandals keep piling up. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned after the Wall Street Journal reported she asked a donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill.
Adviser Corey Lewandowski faces a Justice Department inquiry. The New York Times says Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, agreed to a $50 million deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who later received a pardon.
Trump’s answer was to warn that dishonest allies “have to be prosecuted,” while his Justice Department charged a Virginia Democrat, state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Expect few convictions. Experts point to the Supreme Court: McDonnell in 2016 narrowed “official acts,” Snyder in 2024 excused gratuities paid after the fact, and Trump v. United States granted presidents sweeping immunity.
The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section was effectively shut down in February 2025. What remains, some prosecutors say, is “slime, not crime,” despite overwhelming evidence of corruption that Americans across party lines can no longer ignore.
Nine days to judgment
Voters have noticed anyway. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found nearly two in three Americans think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, with most of the rise coming from Republicans and their leaners.
His approval sits at a record low of 33 percent, and Democrats have spent $182 million on corruption ads, more than the last four cycles combined, according to data from the firm AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance calls the charge “laughable.” Trump’s pollster argues undecided voters will still choose on pocketbook issues. Perhaps. But $5 gasoline and a president’s sons selling drones are hard to pull apart.
The deeper question is what the money buys. In Matthew Cole’s account, Kushner held signing rights on an Emirati account while Abu Dhabi wanted the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) dead.
Trump quit the agreement in May 2018. Months after he left office, Saudi Arabia’s sovereign fund gave his firm $2 billion, despite a screening panel finding its due diligence “unsatisfactory in all aspects.”
Today, at least some of the transactions happen in plain sight: Emirati stablecoin purchases, chip exports, drone contracts, and more.

articles.title: Musk shuts Starlink ‘loophole’ that let Kiev ‘kill people’
articles.body:
Kiev abused Starlink to kill – Musk
SpaceX has closed a “loophole” that allowed the Ukrainian military to use the civilian satellite internet network for offensive drone strikes, Elon Musk has announced, telling warmongers who prolong the conflict to “burn in hell.”
The billionaire’s harsh remarks on Saturday come amid a deepening rift between Washington and Kiev, with US President Donald Trump accusing Vladimir Zelensky of repeatedly rejecting opportunities to end the conflict and worsening global fuel shortages by attacking Russian oil infrastructure.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote on X. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
Correct. Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be. Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them. Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week. Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact. Starlink was also crucial to preventing Russia from overrunning Ukraine in the early days of the war, as all other means of communication were destroyed or jammed by Russia. SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR. That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell. End of story.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 24, 2026
The SpaceX CEO distinguished between the commercial Starlink network and Starshield, a separate military-grade system controlled by the US government. “What they decide to do is up to them,” he said.
Musk concluded with a blistering attack on unnamed “warmongers” who keep pushing for war. His criticism echoes Trump’s increasingly harsh rhetoric toward Zelensky, whom the US president has accused of squandering numerous opportunities to negotiate an end to the fighting.
“I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell,” Musk wrote.
The comments follow days of controversy over restrictions imposed on satellite services used by Ukrainian forces. Kiev claimed the slowdown had disrupted drone operations and initially suggested that Washington was responsible.
Trump denied that his administration had ordered the restrictions. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also rejected allegations of Washington’s involvement, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Kiev against escalating the dispute.
Musk stressed that Starlink remains essential to Ukraine’s military communications and battlefield survival. “Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately,” he wrote, adding that the statement was “NOT a threat” but an assessment of the military’s dependence on the network.
On Saturday, Kiev announced that Starlink and Starshield had returned to their previous operating speeds, with Ukrainian officials thanking Trump and other American representatives for helping resolve the disruption.
Earlier this month, the SpaceX chief declared that “Zelensky has gone too far” after the Ukrainian leader called Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease the global diesel crisis a “weak decision.”
Musk has also accused Ukrainian elites of enriching themselves through Western assistance while ordinary Ukrainians are sent to die on the battlefield. He further alleged that some American taxpayer money sent to the country was being laundered back into US political campaigns.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine report deaths and injuries in overnight strikes
articles.body:
At least three people were killed and 16 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russia, while 10 people were injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine, officials from both countries said on Sunday.
In Russia, two people were killed and two seriously injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus belonging to an agricultural enterprise in the village of Borshchovo in the Bryansk region, regional head Yegor Kovalchuk said.
In Belgorod, one person was killed and 14 injured in a large-scale overnight drone attack, regional Governor Alexander Shuvaev said on the Russian social media platform Max.
In Ukraine, 10 people, including three emergency responders, were injured in Russian strikes in Kharkiv and Vinnytsia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Six more people were injured in a Russian strike on a residential five-story building in Vinnytsia, it added.
The attacks sparked fires, and emergency crews came under repeated strikes while responding to the incidents, the service said.
A fire engine tanker was completely destroyed, it added.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces continued overnight strikes against logistics centers, port infrastructure facilities in Ukraine and vessels allegedly carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces.
In Kharkiv, Russian strikes hit the Epicentr logistics center, a distribution center and the Vasyshchevo logistics terminal, it said.
According to the ministry, the facilities were used to store military or dual-use goods intended to support Ukraine's armed forces.
The ministry also claimed that a dry cargo vessel carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces was struck while crossing the sea en route to the port of Chornomorsk.
Russian air defences intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 25 Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
The claims from both sides could not be independently verified.

articles.title: Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
articles.body:
Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
Talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials, hosted by the US in Tampa, Florida, this week, concluded without any breakthroughs, The New Arab reported on Thursday, citing its own sources.
The discussions were held at US Central Command headquarters, the Pentagon's Middle East operations arm. They come as Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon this month, carrying out air strikes and home demolitions in the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Sidon districts.
The New Arab said it was told there was "intransigence in Israeli positions, while the Lebanese side is holding firm to its demands that steps must be reciprocal".
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF), largely funded by the US, has also rejected direct military-to-military coordination with the Israelis, instead preferring a third-party verification mechanism to be employed by the United Nations and allies such as France.
Israel has bombed Lebanon consistently since October 2023, after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel ignited the region.
A November 2024 ceasefire brokered by the former Biden administration did little to curb Israel's insistence that it was targeting Hezbollah leaders and weapons depots across the country, including in the capital, Beirut.
But it wasn't until this year that Israel significantly ramped up its military operations, mounted a ground invasion, and occupied long stretches of the south and east of Lebanon.
Since the US and Israel launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February, which prompted Hezbollah to launch attacks on Israel in defense of its ally, Israel has killed more than 4,300 Lebanese and displaced one million people in the country.
Lebanese officials have prioritized returning the displaced to their lands and demanded a timetable to do so from the Israelis, but there has been no movement on the issue since the US-sponsored framework was signed by the two sides in June.
Lebanon and Israel agreed to a trilateral framework with the Trump administration in Washington earlier this year, following five rounds of talks hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The three countries held what was billed as a historic signing ceremony on 26 June.
Rubio said it was "the beginning of the beginning" in remarks to reporters at the time.
He later added the US would commit $100m in "humanitarian assistance in coordination with the UN" for affected communities, though he did not specify whether it was just for Lebanon or also for northern Israeli border towns.
Rubio said the LAF would be "reimbursed" by the Trump administration to the tune of $30m.
The framework led to the creation of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, which Washington would facilitate.
But the "pilot zones" that the Israelis pledged to withdraw from, in order to allow the LAF to take over, have not been expanded since July, with the Israelis claiming that the LAF have not had the capacity to disarm Hezbollah fighters.
Hezbollah is the key party to the conflict that was not represented in the talks.
It remains the country's most powerful military organization and far outmatches the LAF's capabilities. It was formed in the 1980s in response to the illegal Israeli occupation of Lebanon.
It has insisted that it cannot disarm while Israel remains a threat to Lebanon, and as Israeli officials normalize rhetoric about expanding Israel's borders to the north.

articles.title: Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
articles.body:

Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
Russia supplied China with more than $80 million worth of submarine-related technology and technical documentation, helping Beijing develop its conventional submarine fleet through cooperation that continued after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an October 22 report titled A Marriage of Convenience? by the Washington-based research organization C4ADS, Russia’s Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering conducted 12 shipments to Chinese military procurement agencies and China Shipbuilding and Offshore International Co. (CSOI) between August 2015 and April 2023.
The transfers, valued at more than $80 million, reportedly involved conceptual designs for non-nuclear submarines, testing documentation, and technologies intended to improve underwater stealth.
Two shipments in October 2019 and January 2020 included documents related to submarine testing, particularly cavitation—a phenomenon that generates underwater noise and can make submarines easier to detect.
A maritime security expert consulted by C4ADS assessed that the documentation indicated Russian assistance in evaluating Chinese submarine noise-reduction technologies.
The cooperation also operated in the opposite direction. Between December 2019 and September 2022, CSOI supplied Rubin with submarine testing equipment, including instruments and control-panel components used to evaluate onboard information and control systems.
Documents accompanying a September 2022 shipment also referenced a joint design and manufacturing contract, indicating that technical cooperation continued after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Rubin, a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation, is subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, European Union, and Japan.
China’s conventional submarine fleet has historically relied on Soviet and Russian technology, although Beijing has since developed its own designs. The C4ADS findings indicate that Russian expertise continued to support Chinese submarine development, particularly in acoustic stealth and underwater systems.
Earlier, an October 19 report revealed that Chinese companies had supplied Russia with industrial equipment, engine components, and navigation technology, helping expand production of Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga facility to a reported capacity of more than 3,000 per month.

articles.title: Could Hormuz become America’s Suez?
articles.body:
In 1956, Britain was forced to abandon the Suez Canal and withdraw from Egypt after a humiliating political and financial defeat. The crisis did not end the British Empire overnight, but it exposed the decline of a power that had dominated much of the world for more than two centuries, in an empire on which the sun famously never set. Britain could still fight wars, but it could no longer act as an independent global power without facing the economic and political limits of its strength. Now, nearly seventy years later, the question is whether the war with Iran and the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz could become America’s Suez.
When war becomes too expensive
After Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, Britain, France and Israel launched a military campaign to regain control of the canal and weaken Nasser’s government. Their forces made rapid progress, but the operation soon became a financial and political crisis for London.
The British pound came under heavy pressure, and the Bank of England had to use its dollar reserves to defend the currency. The United States opposed the invasion and refused to provide the financial support Britain needed unless it agreed to stop the operation. On 6th November, Britain accepted a ceasefire. It later withdrew its forces from Egypt.
As the International Monetary Fund’s account of the crisis explains, the pressure on sterling was central to Britain’s decision. The crisis showed that the government could not continue the war without putting its financial position at long-term risk.
The war with Iran could create a similar problem for the United States, although the economic conditions are different. The dollar is far stronger internationally than the pound was in 1956, and the American economy has greater resources. But the comparison is about the cost of sustaining a war when its political goals remain out of reach.
If the war continues without a clear result, the United States will have to spend more on military operations, weapons, logistics and the protection of its forces. At the same time, the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz can raise costs across the global economy. These pressures may gradually make the war harder to justify, especially if Iran can draw the United States into a prolonged conflict with no clear progress toward its goals.
The cost reaches American households
The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem because of its role in the global energy market. Before the war, around one-fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through the strait, along with a major share of global liquefied natural gas shipments. As oil prices rose, gasoline and diesel became more expensive, air travel and shipping costs increased, and the cost of transporting goods went up. This is where the war became a serious domestic problem for the White House. Higher gasoline prices were immediately visible to American households. Families had to spend more to drive for daily activities and higher diesel prices increased the cost of moving goods.
The latest energy-market reports show how difficult this problem can even become. In October 2026, Reuters reported that Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel. Diesel prices in the United States had also risen sharply, adding to domestic political pressure ahead of the midterm elections. The Reuters report on rising oil prices and the prolonged conflict describes the growing challenge for the Trump administration.
High energy prices can also make it harder to control inflation. Transport and production become more expensive, and the effects spread through the economy. If the Federal Reserve keeps interest rates high to control inflation, borrowing becomes more expensive for households and businesses. The government also has to meet the direct cost of the war while paying interest on its existing debt.
Nevertheless, none of these pressures would force Washington to end the war. The key issue is their combined effect over time. If the war continues, energy prices remain high and the United States fails to achieve objectives, the economic cost of continuing may eventually become greater than the expected benefit.
From military leverage to economic limits
A war of attrition changes the way governments calculate success. At the beginning of a conflict, leaders may expect military action to produce a quick political result. If that result does not come, they face a difficult choice: increase the pressure and spend more, or accept that the original goals may be impossible to achieve at an acceptable cost.
This is the danger facing the United States. Washington has the ability to strike Iranian targets and maintain a strong military presence in the region. But the ability to damage does not mean that Iran will accept American demands. If each new round of fighting adds to the cost without producing a decisive political result, the United States will find itself spending more while moving no closer to its goals.
The Strait of Hormuz gives Iran a way to increase this pressure. Disruption to shipping can keep energy markets unstable and raise the economic cost of the conflict well beyond the battlefield. The longer the disruption continues, the more difficult it becomes for Washington to separate its military campaign from its effects on the American economy.
The question is whether the United States can continue to bear the full cost of the conflict if the economic pressure grows while the chance of achieving its objectives declines. At some stage, American administration may conclude that continuing the war will bring more damage than benefit. That would create the conditions for an American retreat. If Washington withdraws without achieving its main goals, the result could be a strategic defeat, even if American forces remain far stronger than Iran’s in conventional military terms.
Why China could benefit
Such an outcome would also affect the wider balance of power. China is already benefiting from a war that consumes American resources, damages Washington’s reputation and reduces its ability to focus on other strategic priorities. Beijing does not need to defeat the United States directly. It can benefit simply by watching Americas useless overstretch. The war also gives China an opportunity to question whether the United States can keep its commitments to allies in Asia. China would also suffer from high energy prices and disruptions to trade. But if the United States emerges from the war with fewer resources, greater economic pressure and damaged credibility, China could gain room to expand its influence without taking on the costs of a direct military confrontation.
This is one reason the outcome of the war matters beyond the Middle East. A costly American withdrawal could affect how allies and rivals judge US power. Countries that depend on Washington for security may question its ability to sustain a long conflict. Rivals may become more willing to challenge American influence in other regions.
Could this be America’s Suez?
The Suez Crisis did not single-handedly end British power. Britain’s relative decline had been developing for decades, and the United States had already become the leading Western power. But Suez made the change unmistakable. Britain had launched a heavy military operation and then had to withdraw under financial and political pressure. But the crisis clearly exposed the limits of its ability to act as a global power.
A similar outcome is possible for the United States in Iran. If the war becomes more costly with time, if energy prices continue to place pressure on American households and businesses, and if Washington cannot achieve its main objectives, the economic logic for continuing the conflict may become increasingly weak. A withdrawal without a clear political achievement would then damage the credibility of American power as a world superpower.
The United States is not Britain in 1956. Its international position will not collapse because of one war. Yet these advantages do not remove the basic problem: US may ruin its credit as super power of current international order.
The real test will come when Washington has to choose between continuing an expensive war and accepting a retreat. If it leaves Iran without achieving its goals, the consequences could extend far beyond the battlefield. The war could become a turning point that speeds up the decline of American order and gives other powers more room to shape the coming international order. Such scenario would be what could make Hormuz America’s Suez.
