articles.title: Trump says US could strike Iran 'tomorrow' or reach 'big, beautiful' deal
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said Washington could strike Iran as soon as “tomorrow,” or reach a “big, beautiful” agreement with Tehran, amid reports that he is weighing renewed attacks on the Islamic Republic.
“We’re thinking about doing it, and maybe tomorrow,” Trump told reporters when asked how far along he was in considering a possible attack.
“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” he added.
Trump said Iran could still avoid further military action by reaching an agreement with the US, noting that “they want to make a deal, but the problem is, will they hold the deal?”
Trump argued that his goal was to prevent Iran from eventually developing a nuclear weapon, saying an earlier US operation involving B-2 bombers would not have been enough to guarantee a lasting outcome.
“I’ve got to make it permanent,” he said. “That’s the only reason I’m doing it.”
Post-election strike plans
The president also said that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz had increased since the war began.
He offered no firm decision on what comes next, instead presenting both military action and negotiations as possible outcomes.
“I may have to finish it off, or maybe they’ll make a deal,” Trump said. “But I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”
Recent reporting, particularly by The New York Times, suggests that US and Israeli military preparations for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections are advancing, with detailed plans for a potentially brief but intensive offensive.
Citing US officials and people briefed on high-level deliberations, the newspaper reported that both militaries have stepped up exercises, including flights through Iraqi airspace to rehearse strike manoeuvres.
Potential targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenals.
The US-Israeli war with Iran, which began in February and led to a wider conflict in the Middle East, remains unresolved despite a ceasefire and an agreement to finalise a peace deal.

articles.title: The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
articles.body:
The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
In Russia, many people, driven by lingering Europhilia and habits formed during the second half of the 20th century, when Western Europe enjoyed a period of relative peace following its defeat, continue to look for signs of its ‘recovery’ and ways to restore relations.
There are forces within Russia that would advocate overcoming the current hostility and there are decent people in Western Europe, too, even if they are increasingly marginalized. But the causes of this outbreak of desperate Russophobia run deep and cannot easily be remedied and overcoming them may require the complete defeat and dismantling of much of the current European elite. But achieving that goal could come at too high a cost.
I shall attempt to analyze the causes of the almost unprecedented hostility towards Russia among the elites of most European countries and offer recommendations for Russian policy towards Western Europe.
I have written more than once that Peter the Great’s journey towards the rest of Europe, which initially brought many benefits, including helping to create some of the world’s greatest literature and music and modernizing the armed forces, continued for a century and a half longer than was necessary or beneficial.
For many centuries, Europe was the principal source of evil in the world, offering endless wars, including two world wars within a single generation, repeated genocides, colonialism, racism and other calamities.
For Russians who grew up in the shadow of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and who internalized a love of Europe, it’s not easy to acknowledge this simple truth and act accordingly.
Russian Europhilia was greatly reinforced when Western Europe, having been overwhelmed by the torrent of evil it had unleashed, became relatively peaceful for a time during the second half of the 20th century. In the USSR, Europhilia was fueled by the everyday hardships of Soviet socialism, contrasted with the far greater material prosperity of the western part of the half-continent.
There are many reasons for the current anti-Russian hysteria. The main one is the all-encompassing, multi-layered crisis that has gripped the western part of Europe and this crisis is particularly painful after decades of relative prosperity and, above all, the euphoria of victory that swept the West following the collapse of the USSR.
That euphoria temporarily obscured the mounting signs of crisis in European economies and societies, which had already become apparent by the end of the 1960s, when a mood of protest was beginning to take hold. And then a miracle happened as the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc provided hundreds of millions of eager new consumers and millions of cheap workers.
From the 2000s onwards, these problems resurfaced with renewed force. A decade later, most Western European countries had fallen into stagnation as inequality began to worsen once again. Living standards for much of the population began to decline, while competitors started pulling ahead, not only the US and China, but also many countries of the Global South.
Euphoria gave way to a sense of failure and European elites are now trying to drown out that feeling by fueling hostility towards Russia.
At the same time, from the end of the 20th century, the consequences of the anti-colonial revolutions of the 1950s and 1960s began to make themselves felt. The flow of resources that Europe had extracted from the rest of the world since the 16th century, and upon which its prosperity and cultural, military, scientific and technological leadership had largely been built, began to dry up.
An unusually long period of relative peace and prosperity brought to the surface some of the worst traits of the European character and heritage as Western Europe began to turn its back on humanism and the desire to serve the common good.
Decades of development in a climate of peace and formal democracy have led to the degradation of the ruling elites because democratic political systems are anti-meritocratic. The majority elect those who resemble themselves, or even those who are worse, and in the best cases, they elect shrewd manipulators.
One of the most significant causes of Western Europe’s current decline, and to a lesser extent, that of other parts of the collective West, is the rejection of faith.
This began with the Age of Enlightenment, which created the conditions for the decline of people who, consciously or unconsciously, set about rejecting the divine, the best within themselves.
I finally realized that Western Europe had taken a sharp and irreversible downward turn in the early 2000s, when following lengthy debates over the European Union’s proposed constitution, it was decided not to mention Christianity as its spiritual foundation.
Losing its footing and falling behind in economic and spiritual competition, Western Europe is reverting to one of the worst traits of its civilization, which is militarism.
The militarization of the economy is seen as one of the principal ways out of economic decline and militarization requires an enemy. As so often before, that enemy has been identified as Russia as the image of the enemy is being inflated practically out of thin air.
We must tell ourselves firmly, we are not Europeans, but an independent northern Eurasian civilization whose external spiritual roots lie in the south and east.
Our traditional religions came to us from the south, from Byzantium, Palestine, and the Arab and Buddhist worlds. Our political culture stems from the east, from two and a half centuries of interaction and conflict with the Great Mongol Empire, of which the territory of modern-day China was historically a part.
The Mongols plundered, but they didn’t suppress religion, language or culture and we would never have become Great Russia, the world’s largest and one of its most culturally, nationally and religiously open countries, united through a rigid vertical hierarchy of power centered on the Russian people and the Russian language, had it not been for the Mongol political and ideological legacy.
From Western Europe, which, relying on its military superiority, took the lead in education during the 17th and 18th centuries, we sought to adopt the European Bologna system.
Yet that system is increasingly anti-meritocratic as it churns out poorly educated people on a mass scale, many of whom are now coming to power. Let me remind you that some of the earliest institutions of higher learning were established in North Africa and Byzantium.
Some of our more affluent fellow citizens still send their children to study in Europe, ‘abroad’, where as I have seen time and again, they often lose more skills and talents than they acquire.
Our military doctrine contains a clear directive and in circumstances of extreme necessity, provides for the possibility of nuclear strikes against key European countries that are fueling anti-Russian hysteria while simultaneously supporting the war in Ukraine.
Our restraint and peacefulness over recent decades have proved counterproductive. They have contributed to the resurgence of the worst aspects of European political culture so Western Europe must therefore face firm deterrence.
But at the same time, we must remember that we are a country of Pushkin, Tchaikovsky, Dostoevsky, and Tvardovsky, as well as Goethe, Dante, Shakespeare, Mozart and countless others.
Culturally, we must not cut ourselves off from Europe. Rather, we must develop and nurture our Asian roots, of which we have foolishly been ashamed.
The main direction of our internal spiritual, economic and political development must be a shift towards Siberia as there, in the east and north, lies Russia’s future.
We must finally acknowledge that we are not an Eastern European civilization, but a northern Eurasian one, among the most open to the world.
We must also recognize, however difficult it may be, that ‘European-ness’, in the present circumstances, is increasingly becoming a sign of intellectual narrow-mindedness and moral duplicity.
And given the current orientation of European elites, it is simply harmful to us, the representatives of the great multinational, multi-confessional and multicultural Russian people.
Our country-civilization must at last become, for all of us, Russian Yakuts, Russian Buryats, Russian Ossetians, Russian Tatars, Russian Belarusians, Russian Great Russians and others, an independent northern Eurasian civilization.
Europe, in its present and foreseeable future condition, must end at our borders.
This however, is not a call for a new Iron Curtain, but for a rational, modern policy directed towards the future.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

articles.title: Bulgaria votes for president in election dominated by Ukraine war and the economy
articles.body:
The campaign has focused on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and an increase in drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast in the Black Sea, as well as rising energy prices and inflation.
Bulgarians are heading to the polls to elect their president on Sunday, in a campaign that has mostly revolved around growing concerns over the economy and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
The vote will be the first major test of Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party since it came out on top in parliamentary elections last April.
Despite a record 27 candidates, the race is expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who is backed by Radev's party and favours dialogue with Moscow while opposing military aid to Ukraine, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties.
Yotova is expected to win between 41% and 47% of the vote, while Gyurov is polling between 28% and 31%.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.
The campaign has focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country.
The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict, while also compelling the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security.
Candidates have also looked to respond to public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet.
Two main candidates among record total of 27
Main frontrunner Yotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria when Rumen Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections, eventually becoming prime minister.
If successful she would become the first woman ever elected president in Bulgaria's history. A win for Yotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Yotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Her main challenger is economist Andrey Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister in the first few months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition.
Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
Polling stations will close at 8 pm local time, after which initial exit polls will be announced while preliminary results are expected on Monday.
Turnout must be above 50%, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Projections have Sunday’s turnout at less than 40%, indicating a likely runoff on 1 November.

articles.title: Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine
articles.body:
A drone attack damaged an industrial facility in Russia’s Perm Krai early on 25 October, injuring five workers, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. Exilenova+ identified the target as the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Berezniki, around 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border.
The reported strike highlights Ukraine’s ability to reach industrial facilities deep inside Russia that support its military-industrial complex.
AVISMA produces titanium materials used in aviation and aerospace manufacturing, including military aircraft, aircraft engines, missiles, and space technology, according to Exilenova+.
Regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said the industrial facility sustained damage but continued operating normally. He said five workers were injured in the attack.
A target deep inside Russia
Perm Krai lies in Russia’s Ural region, roughly 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border. The distance places the reported strike far beyond Russia’s border regions, where Ukrainian drone attacks have frequently targeted military and industrial infrastructure.
The reported attack follows a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russian industrial and energy facilities linked to the country’s war effort.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that air defenses intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones overnight across 23 Russian regions and over the Sea of Azov, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
The reported interceptions included drones over Perm Krai, as well as regions around Moscow and areas in southern and western Russia. The figures have not been independently verified.
The extent of damage at AVISMA and any impact on its operations have not been independently established.

articles.title: Ballistic missile attacks rock Yemen's Aden
articles.body:
ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Loud explosions were heard in Yemen's southern port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government, on Saturday following a ballistic missile attack, a local security official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Houthi group fired nearly four ballistic missiles at the city, with some striking near Aden International Airport and key military facilities in the Khormaksar district, and another hitting the Coast Guard Troops headquarters in Al-Tawahi district.
The blasts shook buildings across parts of Aden, residents told Xinhua, with plumes of smoke seen rising from the targeted areas. Casualties and damage were not immediately known.
The attack marked the latest in a series of Houthi missile strikes on Aden. On Wednesday, the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike on a Saudi military operations room at Badr military base near Aden International Airport.
Earlier this month, strikes hit the airport grounds, a military base in the Al-Buraiqa district, and the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound. The government said the Oct. 15 attack on the palace compound killed five people and wounded 16 others.
The renewed strikes come amid intensified fighting between the Houthis and government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition. Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

articles.title: National Guard Drones Deliver 600 kg of Aid to Occupied Oleshky
articles.body:
Ukrainian National Guard operators have deployed unmanned aerial vehicles to deliver over 600 kilograms of humanitarian aid, infant food, and toys to families trapped in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
The aerial resupply mission was executed by service members of the “Bolharychi” special purpose company, a subordinate unit of the 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine, state news agency Ukrinform reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Writing on Facebook, Vyhivskyi confirmed that unmanned aerial platforms transported 15 individual cargo containers across contested airspace into the isolated Dnipro left-bank enclave in the southern Kherson region.
“Despite the Russian occupation and the severe conditions confronting the residents of Kherson region, our units continue to support the people,” Vyhivskyi stated in an official dispatch.
Critical aid shipments
The delivered cargo focused primarily on life-sustaining supplies for households with young children facing acute shortages of infant nutrition and basic necessities.
According to the internal affairs minister, the 15 airdropped consignments contained baby milk formula, breakfast cereals, dried foods, developmental games, and toys for infants and toddlers isolated under military occupation.
“Among the children who remain in blocked Oleshky are those born during the full-scale war who have known no life without terror,” Vyhivskyi said.
Russian Drone Hits Vinnytsia Apartment Block, 6 Injured
“We support these families and deliver essential basic goods to them.”
Vyhivskyi expressed formal gratitude to the volunteer logistics networks that assembled the care packages, the drone operators who navigated contested electronic warfare corridors, the armed detachments providing fire cover, and local contacts on the ground who risked their lives to recover and distribute the supplies within the occupied perimeter.
Humanitarian crisis in the left-bank enclave
The drone delivery underscores the desperate conditions in Oleshky, situated approximately five kilometers southeast of liberated Kherson on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
The municipality has remained under Russian military control since the opening days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and has been entirely severed from authorized overland cargo deliveries and international humanitarian missions since late May.
Roughly 1,700 civilians remain trapped in the municipal center amid destroyed municipal heating networks, severed running water, and intermittent electrical supply ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described the municipality as under virtual siege, noting that exit roads and river transit points are heavily mined and subjected to continuous loitering drone reconnaissance.
Ukrainian defense units have intermittently utilized heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop rations and pharmaceuticals into residential yards as diplomatic negotiations to secure an overland corridor continue.
Pending localized ceasefire
The aerial relief mission coincides with preparations for a synchronized, localized ceasefire framework scheduled to take effect across Oleshky on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time (4:00 a.m. Moscow time).
Finalized during bilateral consultations between Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and Russian negotiating lead Yana Lantratova – mediated with assistance from US First Lady Melania Trump – the framework establishes a phased humanitarian operation to deliver larger medical and food consignments and begin civilian evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky affirmed that Kyiv will adhere strictly to operational commitments to unblock the city, emphasizing that opening humanitarian access to Oleshky remains vital to preventing catastrophic civilian loss ahead of winter.

articles.title: Iran-allied Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites, strikes reported on Yemen’s Aden
articles.body:
Iran-allied Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites, strikes reported on Yemen’s Aden
- The Iran-allied Houthis said they attacked Saudi oil sites and airports, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and Aramco sites in Yanbu and Rabigh.
- The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif, while Yemen’s government said Houthi missiles hit coast guard sites in Aden.
- The fighting has broken a 2022 UN-brokered truce and widened tensions in the region, with Saudi Civil Defence briefly warning people in Taif, Yanbu, Mecca and Jeddah.
AI generated
RIYADH - Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Oct 24, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the Houthi reports, and it was not immediately clear if the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif on Saturday.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis’ missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group’s forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Oct 24, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom’s second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom. REUTERS

articles.title: Preparations Underway for Putin-Trump-Xi Trilateral Summit, Ushakov Says
articles.body:
Preparations have commenced for a trilateral summit bringing together Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
Speaking to Russian state television network Vesti and reported by news outlet Astra, Ushakov confirmed that Moscow, Beijing, and Washington have agreed in principle to convene the three-way leader-level meeting.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Right now, I can already state definitely that Moscow, Beijing, and Washington are in principle ready to hold it, and preparations for it have already begun,” Ushakov said.
The senior Kremlin aide indicated that the trilateral summit is being planned to take place on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit scheduled for Nov. 18–19 in Shenzhen, China.
Addressing parallel diplomatic tracks, Ushakov characterized a prospective three-way meeting involving delegations from the Russia, the US and Ukraine in November as exploratory in nature, describing it as having a “range-finding character.”
APEC summit and conditions for Miami G20 attendance
Ushakov also addressed the possibility of Vladimir Putin attending the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, Florida, scheduled for December, confirming that the Kremlin has received a formal invitation to the gathering from Washington.
However, the aide stated that Putin’s prospective travel to the United States remains contingent upon the operational progress and concrete diplomatic outcomes achieved during the November APEC meetings in Shenzhen.
Drones Hit Omsky Kauchuk Deep in Russia, Belgorod Targeted
“For now, we are discussing the November summit in Shenzhen, but we have received an invitation,” Ushakov stated regarding the Miami G20 invitation.
Asked directly whether the decision regarding Putin’s travel to Florida depends significantly on the success of the trilateral summit in China, Ushakov answered affirmatively.
“Of course. But as I say: first comes November, and then comes December,” Ushakov emphasized, underscoring that diplomatic sequencing will dictate Moscow’s scheduling determinations.
Diplomatic controversy and international legal hurdles
The prospect of direct leader-level engagements involving Trump, Putin, and Xi unfolds amid acute sensitivity across European capitals regarding great-power diplomacy brokered without the direct participation of affected European partners and Ukraine.
Former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk cautioned on Saturday that three-way arrangements between Washington, Moscow, and Beijing risk partitioning European security architectures, comparing prospective summitry without Ukraine to the 1938 Munich Agreement and the 1945 Yalta Conference.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has consistently stressed that no diplomatic architecture affecting Ukraine’s sovereignty or borders can be concluded over Kyiv’s head.
The Kremlin’s confirmation of the Miami invitation also intersects with institutional pushback from EU officials and international legal bodies.
European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas and the European Commission have repeatedly criticized White House overtures toward the Russian head of state, citing state-sponsored hybrid sabotage operations across Europe and an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague charging Putin with war crimes connected to the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Starlink speeds restored after week of frontline disruption
articles.body:
Musk admits he throttled Ukraine’s Starlink speeds, as access is restored
The SpaceX CEO says Kyiv’s forces had used the civilian commercial service for deadly offensive drone strikes
Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.
Musk’s admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks.
“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said on social media, adding that restoration began overnight and was sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

articles.title: Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
articles.body:
Iran slams US-Israeli attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, condemns double standards
TEHRAN– Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations has condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, accusing Western countries and international nuclear authorities of applying double standards and politicizing global non-proliferation efforts.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday, Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, reaffirmed Iran’s inalienable right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including uranium enrichment.
Darzi said the United States was challenging the rights of NPT member states by questioning their entitlement to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle. He argued that denying countries access to uranium enrichment technology while claiming to support peaceful nuclear energy was incompatible with Article IV of the treaty.
“No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties,” he said, warning against the use of non-proliferation concerns as a means of exerting political pressure on sovereign nations.
The Iranian envoy said the United States and Israel had launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards. He described the attacks as violations of international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions and UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981).
According to Darzi, the attacks caused extensive destruction and claimed thousands of lives, including that of Iran’s Leader, whose religious decree, or fatwa, rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction.
Iran criticizes international response
Darzi strongly criticized the IAEA’s governing bodies, its director general and the UN Security Council for failing to condemn the attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities. He said the absence of a clear response had exposed the selective application of international non-proliferation standards.
“Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the treatment of Iran, an NPT member since 1970, with that of Israel, which he described as the only nuclear-armed state in the region and whose nuclear facilities are not subject to comprehensive IAEA safeguards.
He argued that continued political and military pressure on Iran, alongside 'impunity for Israel,' undermined the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime. He also criticized the withholding of technical cooperation that, in his view, deprived Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the IAEA is mandated to promote.
Safety conditions remain central to inspections
Addressing calls for the resumption of inspections, Darzi said Iran had neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, he stressed that the military attacks had fundamentally changed the physical and security conditions under which verification activities could take place.
He noted that the IAEA’s own reports acknowledged that verification activities had ceased and inspectors had been withdrawn for safety reasons. Such concerns, he said, could not be disregarded when demands were made for their return.
“No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees,” Darzi said, adding that responsibility for creating these conditions rested with the countries that carried out the attacks.
He concluded that Iran remained prepared to cooperate with the IAEA to the extent permitted by prevailing circumstances, but emphasized that such cooperation must not compromise the safety of the Iranian people, nuclear facilities or agency inspectors.
Darzi also insisted that the IAEA’s reporting must remain professional, objective and free from political influence, arguing that the agency’s credibility depended on technical integrity and impartiality.

articles.title: Putin dismisses claims Russia is fueling European protests as ‘clear overkill’
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed accusations that Moscow is orchestrating mass protests in major European cities as a “clear overkill,” accusing European leaders of blaming external powers rather than confronting the causes of domestic unrest.
In an interview with the VGTRK broadcasting company published on Sunday, Putin said he was initially surprised that European criticism over the demonstrations focused on the United States before shifting towards Russia.
“Claims immediately began to be thrown out that the events taking place in Europe are the result of the activities of the current American administration and its support for right-wing parties and movements,” he said.
Putin described that reaction as “strange and completely unexpected,” saying he had not anticipated European leaders would criticise the United States, which he called their main military ally and protector.
He added that European leaders had subsequently returned to what he described as their “traditional accusations” against Russia.
Putin accuses European leaders of shifting blame
Putin argued that allegations of Russian involvement in mass demonstrations were exaggerated and said European governments were avoiding responsibility for the unrest.
“My first reaction when I saw this was surprise, because to say that we are provoking mass protests in major European cities is a clear overkill,” he said, adding that the claim should be obvious to ordinary European citizens.
The Russian president said the accusations reflected what he described as the weakness of some European leaders, arguing that they were blaming Washington and Moscow rather than analysing the underlying causes of public discontent.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected allegations of Russian interference in European political affairs.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also dismissed the accusations as “absurd” on October 19, according to reports.
France protests fuel dispute over foreign influence
The remarks come amid weeks of nationwide student protests in France, where debate over the demonstrations has increasingly extended to allegations of outside influence.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, speaking at an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development-hosted conference on October 21, accused protesters of drawing on what he described as “hostile narratives” associated with Russia, China, Iran and the MAGA movement.

articles.title: Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Thousands protest against Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election (VIDEO)
A major protest against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has taken place in Tel-Aviv just days ahead of the Israeli parliamentary election on October 27.
A square outside the Museum of Art in the country’s largest city was packed on Saturday evening, with the demonstrators holding national flags and banners, reading ‘Change will come’, ‘No more Mr. Far Right Guy’ and other slogans.
The organizers of the gathering from the October Council group put the attendance at over 100,000. The police have yet to announce official figures.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the election – Yashar party chairman and former military chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot – and other leaders of the opposition bloc have attended the rally. The crowd cheered Eisenkot’s appearance, chanting: “Who’s coming? The next prime minister.”
The October Council was formed by families of the victims of the attack on Israel by Hamas on October 7, 2023, who demand accountability from Netanuahy’s right-wing government for the failure to prevent the incursion.
Saturday’s protest, organized with the title ‘In Three Days, Vote for a State Commission of Inquiry’, is the culmination of three years of weekly rallies, according to the group.
The State Commissions of Inquiry, which are independent panels appointed by the Supreme Court, are usually set up in Israel to investigate major failures by the authorities. However, Netanyahu refused to establish such a probe into October 7, insisting that it would be biased against his government.
Reports in the US and local media claimed that the prime minister ignored warnings of the planned attack by Hamas he had received from various sources, including Israeli intelligence and the UAE and Egypt. Netanyahu has denied those claims.
A poll by public broadcaster KAN published before the start of the election silence period on Friday, suggested that Eisenkot’s opposition bloc would get 52 out of 120 in the Israeli parliament, with Netanyahu and his supporters winning 50 seats. This means that neither is likely control the Knesset outright.
Israel responded to the October 7 incursion by Hamas, in which 1,200 people lost their lives and around 250 were taken hostage, by launching a military campaign in Gaza.
Israeli airstrikes and a ground offensive have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, and injured over 175,000 others in the enclave over the past three years, according to the local Health Ministry. More than 1,500 deaths happened after a US-brokered ceasefire went into effect in October 2025.

articles.title: “Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more
articles.body:
Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
German MEP from the Greens Danie Freund:
“Strasbourg Calling”: Europe must produce the right things, not simply more
Interview with MEP Daniel Freund
Sunday 25 October 2026 13:06
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 13:06
MEP Daniel Freund
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
At its Strasbourg session this week, the European Parliament discussed the conclusions of last week's European Council meeting. However, the major issue of the EU's long-term budget for 2028-2034 remains unresolved. Europe wants to become a geopolitical power, rearm, compete with China and maintain its climate targets. But who will pay for it all?
German Green MEP Daniel Freund, the Greens' coordinator on the Committee on Budgetary Control, warns that Europe cannot take on more responsibilities with less money and must not abandon its climate targets.
Speaking on BNR's special  broadcast from Strasbourg, he said:
“Europe still has a great deal to do in terms of defence, support for Ukraine and competition with China. I see our chancellor, as well as members of my own party, calling for substantial budget cuts. Fuel prices keep rising, driven by our dependence on fossil fuels and the problems involving Iran.
I think we are currently seeing some of the highest prices ever at petrol pumps and filling stations. At the same time, we are seeing a major increase in electric vehicle use. In Denmark, for example, electric vehicles already account for 80% of new car sales, while in Germany the figure is 30%. So I think we need to move in that direction.”
MEP Daniel Freund and BNR's Irina Nedeva in the Radio Studios complex at the European Parliament in Strasbourg (21 October 2026)
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
Italy, Greece, Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are preparing a petition calling for a further postponement or weakening of the emissions trading scheme. Europe must nevertheless maintain its climate targets, the politician insisted in an interview with BNR Horizon's programme “Strasbourg Calling”:
“We do not want to keep spending billions to support petrol producers, these huge companies, and in doing so also support dictators. We want to put an end to that! We want to continue transforming our economies and making them increasingly green. This summer, we saw 32,000 Europeans lose their lives during heatwaves. And yet it was the coolest summer compared with those forecast to come. So we certainly need to keep moving in this direction.”
Daniel Freund argued that decarbonisation is not incompatible with industrial competitiveness:
“We can already see what is happening in China. The Chinese market has stopped buying cars with internal combustion engines from us, and only electric vehicles are being used. The same applies to other products. So if we want to remain competitive, we need to offer the right products. For example, companies that use electric trucks and renewable energy are not currently being affected by the fuel crisis.”
Europe must strengthen its defence industry, but even defence is becoming greener, he noted:
“Even if we look at the battlefield in Ukraine, we can see that this war is being fought, to some extent, using renewable energy. A large number of drones are being deployed, and they operate on batteries. What we must do is stand together in defending Ukraine, because in doing so we are fighting for our shared values and our own survival.”
The Greens will support the European Parliament resolution aimed at strengthening security in the Black Sea in response to Russian threats, he added:
“I think we will support the resolution. We stand with Bulgaria, Romania and every country that falls victim to such Russian attacks.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Daniel Freund was aired on BNR's Horizon channel on October 21 and can be heard HERE.

articles.title: Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
articles.body:
Twelve countries condemn any attack or threat against nuclear facilities
TEHRAN – Twelve countries, including Iran, Russia, China and Pakistan, have issued a joint statement declaring that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
On Friday, the 12 countries — Belarus, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Eritrea, Iran, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe — issued the joint statement during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee. The statement addressed the prohibition of any attack or threat of attack against nuclear sites and facilities that are under the safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
According to IRNA, the statement was read out by Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations. It contained eight points, as follows:
1. We reaffirm the importance of the full and effective fulfilment of the objectives of the International Atomic Energy Agency, particularly its statutory mission to accelerate and enlarge the contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. We also reaffirm the inalienable right of all states to develop research into, produce and use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination.
2. We recall United Nations Security Council Resolution 487 (1981), which strongly condemned a military attack against nuclear facilities. We also recall the relevant decisions and resolutions of the IAEA General Conference — documents GC(53)/DEC/13, GC(XXIX)/RES/443, GC(XXIX)/RES/444 and GC(XXXIV)/RES/533 — which clearly reflect the longstanding position of the international community opposing any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards and dedicated to peaceful purposes.
3. We reaffirm that an attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities violates the principles of the United Nations Charter, international law and the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and is fundamentally incompatible with the objectives and purposes of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
4. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities have serious implications for nuclear safety and security and pose a grave threat to the integrity, effectiveness and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, as well as to the broader global non-proliferation framework.
5. We emphasize that attacks against nuclear facilities would adversely affect the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation, and could result in the release of radioactive materials, with severe consequences both within and beyond the affected country, including serious impacts on civilian populations and long-term environmental damage.
6. We emphasize that silence in the face of attacks against protected nuclear facilities undermines established international norms, erodes confidence in the international legal order and increases the risk of such attacks becoming normalised.
7. We therefore reaffirm that nuclear facilities must never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or the threat of attack.
8. We call on all member states to stand united in preserving the integrity and credibility of the IAEA safeguards system, strengthening nuclear safety and security, and protecting the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and international cooperation by expressing their clear and unequivocal opposition to any attack or threat of attack against nuclear facilities.

articles.title: EU extends sanctions against Jacques Baud
articles.body:
EU extends sanctions against Jacques Baud
The European Union has extended the sanctions against Jacques Baud, a former colonel in the Swiss Army General Staff, who is accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda, until October 9, 2027. He remains subject to an asset freeze and travel restrictions.
According to official EU documents reported by the French-speaking Swiss online media outlet L’Impertinent, on October 8 the Council of the European Union renewed the sanctions regime against Russia’s “destabilising activities”, which targets 80 individuals and 20 entities.
Added to this list on December 15, 2025, the 71-year-old Brussels resident is accused of his contributions to media outlets described as pro-Russian and of spreading “conspiracy theories”. The EU Council criticises him in particular for accusing Ukraine of having orchestrated its own invasion in order to join NATO.
Initially, Brussels accused him of supporting Russian actions that “undermine or threaten the stability or security of a third country (Ukraine)”. The new text now refers to actions that “undermine democracy and threaten the stability or security of a third country”. Ukraine is no longer explicitly mentioned, and the conjunction “or” has been replaced by “and”. The specific allegations remain unchanged. The EU has not provided any justification for the rewording.
The individual concerned disputes the allegations: “I have never received a single cent from Russia,” he stated in December 2025, notably in an interview with L’Impertinent. The 71-year-old claims to base his analyses on Ukrainian and American sources and disputes, in particular, the interpretation of his statements regarding the Russian invasion. In his view, these statements referred to an interview given in 2019 by Oleksiy Arestovych, who was to become an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Baud brought a case before the General Court of the EU last March seeking the annulment of his inclusion on the list.
+ Switzerland approves 20th sanctions package against Russia
A retired colonel of the General Staff, born in Geneva, Jacques Baud worked for the Swiss secret services from 1983 to 1990, where he was responsible for analysing Warsaw Pact forces. He subsequently held various posts with the UN, notably in Sudan.
Highly critical of the EU’s and Western countries’ policies on the war in Ukraine, Baud has a large online following, particularly on YouTube, where his videos have racked up several million views.
The sanctions are having a serious impact on his daily life. Baud can no longer freely access his bank accounts, particularly to access his pension. He also claims he is unable to leave Belgium.
After several months of restrictions, a humanitarian exemption had allowed him to regain access to his Belgian account from mid-March to the end of June. Since the beginning of July, he says, the funds have once again been inaccessible. A new exemption requested at the start of May was granted by the Belgian authorities at the start of October, but by the middle of the month it had still not been implemented.

articles.title: Houthi militia launches multiple missile attacks on Yemen's Aden
articles.body:
Yemeni authorities have said that the Houthi militia targeted Aden International Airport, a port in the city’s al-Tawahi district and two coast guard facilities with ballistic missiles.
The information ministry reported renewed ballistic missile attacks on the airport and port in a post on X on Saturday, without providing details on casualties or damage.
Separately, the interior ministry said two ballistic missiles targeted the coast guard headquarters at the ministry’s compound, while a third targeted a coast guard building in the al-Tawahi district. 
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government have come under sustained attack from the Houthi militia.
The Saudi-led coalition said earlier it intercepted two missiles targeting the western Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu before explosions were heard in Aden.
The Houthi militia quickly claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it had targeted a naval base and a military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
Houthi militia military spokesperson Yahya Saree said its forces targeted Saudi troops at Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden.
His statement did not mention Aden International Airport or specify the weapons used.
The interior ministry said the strikes came after previous attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Aden, including repeated ballistic missile and drone attacks on the international airport.
It warned that targeting vital facilities and public infrastructure threatened the city’s security and stability, endangered civilians and affected institutions providing security and public services.
The Yemeni government and its allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces, while the Houthi militia control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Houthi militia since 2015.
Recent escalation between Yemen's government forces and the Houthi militia began in July as a 2022 ceasefire collapsed. 
The group has also targeted Saudi Arabia's energy and civilian sites.

articles.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
articles.body:
Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.
Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.
The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported.
Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.
In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.
After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.
Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.
The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.
State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections."
Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.
Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.
Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."
SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE
Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.
The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions.
Moraes did not respond to a comment request.
Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.
Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court.
Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.
Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.
Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.
Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.
The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.
A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."
TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS
The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.
Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.
In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.
Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.
Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.
The State Department announced the designation the following day.
Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.
BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS
In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.
Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.
Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said.
Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.
Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.
Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.
"Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually." REUTERS

articles.title: Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant
articles.body:
Russian embassy denies reports of staff leaving Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant
TEHRAN – The Russian Embassy in Tehran has dismissed reports that Russian diplomatic staff and specialists working at Iran’s Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving the country, stressing that activities are continuing as usual.
In a statement, the embassy said it was aware of reports published by certain hostile media outlets alleging that an evacuation of Russian embassy personnel and specialists at the Bushehr facility was underway.
“We would like to clarify that neither embassy staff nor Russian specialists at the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are leaving Iran,” the statement said.
The embassy emphasized that operations were proceeding as normal, describing contrary reports as false information and saying their origins were entirely clear.
Located on Iran’s southern coast along the Persian Gulf, the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant is Iran’s first commercial nuclear power facility. Although construction at the site was initially undertaken by the German company Siemens in the 1970s, Russia took responsibility for completing the plant’s first reactor unit under an agreement signed with Iran in the 1990s. The first unit was connected to Iran’s national electricity grid in 2011 and reached full capacity in 2013.
Russia has continued to cooperate with Iran on the development of the facility, including the construction of additional reactor units. The project forms part of broader cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

articles.title: IDF kills two terrorists who funneled millions from Iran and Turkey to Hamas
articles.body:
The IDF announced Sunday that it had killed two terrorists in separate airstrikes in the Gaza Strip last week, accusing them of transferring millions of shekels from Iran and Turkey to Hamas' military wing throughout the war. According to the military, the funds were used to help the terrorist organization rebuild its military capabilities and prepare attacks against Israeli soldiers and civilians.
The first terrorist, Alaa Ibrahim Nimer Arshi, a cell commander in Hamas' military wing, was killed in an airstrike in the Gaza City area. The second, Karam Riyad Hassan Abu Butaihan, a Palestinian Islamic Jihad terrorist who helped transfer money to Hamas, was killed in the Nuseirat area in central Gaza.
According to the IDF, both men played a role in channeling funds to Hamas throughout the war, including money originating from Iran and Turkey. The military said the financial transfers had recently supported Hamas' efforts to restore its military infrastructure and advance attacks against Israeli forces and civilians.
In a separate operation last week, the IDF and Shin Bet security agency carried out an airstrike in central Gaza, destroying a weapons depot used by Hamas to store military equipment. The facility contained Kalashnikov rifles, a launcher and rockets, according to the military.
Additional terrorists killed in Gaza strikes
The announcement follows an IDF statement last week confirming the deaths of two additional terrorists in separate strikes.
One was Akram Bassam Shaaban Yassin, a senior member of Hamas' General Security apparatus in the Gaza Strip. The other was Tamer Mohammed Ibrahim al-Sabbagh, whom the military identified as a member of the terrorist cell responsible for abducting and murdering German-Israeli citizen Shani Louk during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

articles.title: Russian Strike Hits Epicentr Mall in Poltava, Woman Injured
articles.body:
A Russian aerial strike struck the Epicentr shopping center in the central city of Poltava on Sunday, Oct. 25, igniting a fire across the commercial building and injuring a 52-year-old woman, regional authorities reported.
Head of the Poltava Regional Military Administration Vitalii Diakivnych announced on Telegram that incoming fire struck the large retail center, triggering an immediate blaze and causing structural damage.

“A fire broke out. Information regarding the extent of the damage is being clarified. Liquidation of the consequences of the attack is ongoing. Preliminarily, a 52-year-old woman sustained injuries,” Diakivnych stated.
Emergency responders, specialized firefighting brigades, and civil defense units deployed to the site of the hit to contain the blaze, secure the perimeter, and evaluate whether additional personnel or visitors were inside the facility during the impact.
Weekend infrastructure strikes
The kinetic impact on the Epicentr hypermarket in Poltava follows a sequence of targeted Russian strikes against commercial retail sites, logistics facilities, and public infrastructure across Ukraine over the weekend.
On Saturday evening, Russian forces struck a commercial shopping center in the Osnovianskyi district of Kharkiv, igniting a major structural blaze, alongside strikes on a construction hypermarket and industrial facilities that wounded several civilians and three emergency rescue workers during follow-on secondary strikes.
4 Killed in Synelnykove Strike, Rescuers Hit in Kharkiv
Concurrently in Dnipropetrovsk region, a strike drone hit a residential high-rise in Synelnykove, killing four civilians and wounding 13 others.
Overnight into Sunday, Russian bombardments damaged critical infrastructure and municipal utility networks across nine regions, with impacts reported at thermal power plants, electrical substations, coal mining enterprises, grain storage facilities, and a postal depot.

articles.title: Trump wants 'business with both' Ukraine, Russia after war ends
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 24 that he sees the U.S. doing business with both Ukraine and Russia after the war ends, despite criticism of efforts to restore commercial ties with Moscow.
The statement comes as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel is heading to New York from the Baltic port of Primorsk, set to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel following a supply agreement Trump announced on Oct. 9.
Soon after the announcement, Moscow partially lifted restrictions on its diesel exports, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons.
"Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think," Trump said.
Trump added that he wanted to "get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both."
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have secured greater financial returns in exchange for the billions of dollars in aid provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden's presidency.
"I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid," Trump said.
Plans to import around 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel in the coming months have drawn criticism of the Trump administration from European allies, Ukraine, and members of Congress, as the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The shipment would mark the first Russian diesel deliveries to the U.S. since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
The deal comes amid a growing rift between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine faces restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump has also stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing him of being unwilling to end the war and calling for his replacement.
The decision to resume Russian diesel imports coincides with a challenging political landscape for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polls showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance, marking the lowest approval rating of either of his presidential terms.
Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would vote for Democrats if congressional elections were held today, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead — their largest of the current election cycle.

articles.title: Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
articles.body:
Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
With Americans struggling from soaring energy prices, and businesses across the country trying to keep their heads above water, the Democrats’ apparent priority is to threaten companies that might help ease the pressure.
According to an October 22 Washington Post report, Senate Democrats are preparing to investigate American companies involved in US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee has reportedly asked businesses to preserve relevant documents ahead of possible congressional investigations, should Democrats regain control of Congress in the November midterms.
For a party that claims to champion working Americans, this is a peculiar way of demonstrating its concern.
Diesel is the lifeblood of the American economy. It powers the trucks that carry food to supermarkets, the tractors that harvest crops, the machinery that builds homes and roads, and the locomotives that move freight across the vast country.
Yet the people who depend on it have too often been treated as an afterthought by the Washington establishment. They live and work in the industrial towns, farming communities and sprawling rural counties that coastal political elites dismiss as flyover country.
Just recall Hillary Clinton’s infamous 2016 description of millions of Trump supporters as a “basket of deplorables” – a perfect crystallization of the contempt that many ordinary Americans felt was directed at them by the Democrats.
A decade later, that perception is unlikely to be helped by the Democratic lawmakers’ threats to investigate businesses for participating in an arrangement intended to bring additional fuel to the market.
The timing makes those threats extra galling. America is facing an energy crunch aggravated by the Trump administration’s own military campaign against Iran. There is no reason to pretend otherwise. Yes, the president’s decisions helped disrupt global energy markets, and Americans are entitled to demand answers about their consequences.
But recognizing that responsibility does not mean opposing every subsequent attempt to alleviate the damage.
Trump’s decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel represents an effort to increase available supplies at a time when the market desperately needs relief. It is a pragmatic response to an immediate economic problem, whatever one thinks of the circumstances that created it.
And now Democrats are determined to make that response costly for the companies willing to participate.
Congress has every right to examine whether the administration acted within its legal authority. But threatening private businesses with investigations for engaging in transactions authorized by the federal government is another matter entirely. If those companies comply with the law, why should they have to fear becoming targets of a future congressional majority?
The actual volume of Russian diesel involved is almost beside the point. Moscow initially pledged to release some 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with further shipments promised in the following months – a modest quantity compared to America’s enormous fuel consumption.
But that’s not what the markets will be reacting to. They react to expectations, regulatory certainty and the willingness of businesses to undertake transactions without fearing political retaliation. And now, even a lawful, government-authorized energy deal could expose companies to years of investigations simply because a different party took power.
Just imagine the chilling effect.
Today, the dispute concerns a relatively small quantity of fuel from one supplier. Tomorrow, the same approach could be applied to other commodities, trading partners or commercial arrangements that fall afoul of Washington’s shifting ideological priorities.
In effect, the Democrats want to hold American energy security hostage to domestic political warfare.
And for what? The ostensible objective is to keep pressuring Russia.
For years, Moscow has faced sweeping Western sanctions, restrictions on financial transactions and efforts to shut its energy exports out of international markets. None of this has forced Russia to accept any of the West’s demands.
Russia has shown it can adapt and endure economic pressure. While not entirely painless, sanctions have consistently failed to produce the political outcome their advocates have called and hoped for.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly signaled that it remains prepared to negotiate to reasonable counterparts that would take Russia’s own security concerns and national interests into account. Whether those positions are acceptable to Washington is a matter for diplomacy – and refusing to talk altogether is not diplomacy.
Trump is willing to acknowledge that Russia remains a major power with which the US must eventually find a workable relationship. It’s the baseline level of recognition of political reality one expects from the leader of a major world power.
What the Democrats are doing is the international-politics equivalent of pressing their hands to their ears and shouting ‘La La La’ at the top of their lungs.
The truck driver paying more at the pump, the farmer counting operating costs for the next season and the small-business owner watching expenses climb have little interest in Washington’s political theater. They want affordable fuel, predictable costs and a government that remembers whom it is supposed to serve.
Threatening investigations to discourage companies from helping supply the American market is not sending the message the Democrats seem to think it’s sending. It suggests that, to them, political obedience matters more than keeping the country running.
And ordinary Americans could once again be left paying the bill.

articles.title: BSF apprehends four Pakistani fishermen in Kutch, seizes boat
articles.body:
The Border Security Force (BSF) has apprehended four Pakistani fishermen who allegedly entered Indian waters for crab-catching activities and seized a fishing boat near the India-Pakistan border in Gujarat’s Kutch district.According to news agency PTI, the fishermen were apprehended from the Sir Creek area on Sunday following specific intelligence inputs, an official said. The fishermen were identified as Kadir Thaimor, Muhammad Mussa, Azgar Thaimor and Ahsan Jat, all residents of Chach Jaan Khan village in Pakistan’s Sindh province, according to information provided by the BSF.Sir Creek is a narrow, marshy tidal channel in the Rann of Kutch, along the coastal region between Gujarat and Pakistan’s Sindh province. The area is strategically sensitive because the longstanding India-Pakistan boundary dispute over the creek affects the demarcation of the maritime boundary in the Arabian Sea.The region’s shallow waters, tidal channels and extensive marshlands make navigation and border surveillance challenging. Fishing activities in the area can also lead to fishermen crossing into the other country’s waters, prompting apprehensions by security personnel.
The BSF maintains surveillance along the sensitive western border to prevent unauthorised crossings and other illegal activities. The latest apprehension follows an operation based on specific intelligence inputs, during which the four fishermen and their boat were taken into custody.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.
