articles.title: Royal Navy moves to buy U.S.-made Skydio X10D drones
articles.body:
- Britain’s Ministry of Defence opened a tender for Skydio X10D reconnaissance drones with an estimated value of about $160,700 excluding VAT.
- Bids are due Nov. 19, and the contract is set to run until March 31, 2027.
Britain’s Ministry of Defence has opened a tender to buy Skydio X10D small drones, the American-made reconnaissance quadcopter already ordered by the thousands by the U.S. Army, with an estimated budget of £120,000 (about $160,700) excluding VAT, according to a notice on the Defence Sourcing Portal.
The tender was issued by Navy Commercial, the Royal Navy’s procurement office at Whale Island in Portsmouth, and published on Oct. 20 under the Procurement Act 2023. It does not say how many drones the ministry plans to buy or which unit will operate them. Delivery is listed for the South-East of England.
The contract is short. Bids are due by Nov. 19, the ministry expects to pick a supplier around Nov. 26, and the formal notice lists the contract as running from Nov. 30, 2026, to March 31, 2027, the end of the British government’s financial year. The listing on the Defence Sourcing Portal gives a slightly later start date of Dec. 10. The tender is open to any qualifying supplier, is marked as suitable for small and medium-sized businesses, and will be decided on price.
The X10D is a compact, rucksack-portable quadcopter built by Skydio in Hayward, California, for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. It carries day and thermal cameras, uses onboard artificial intelligence to fly itself around obstacles, including in complete darkness, and can track a subject day or night. The drone can switch radio channels automatically to keep its link under jamming and is designed to hold its position without relying on GPS.
The X10D has been on the U.S. Department of War’s Blue UAS list of drones cleared for military use since May 2024. In March, the U.S. Army ordered more than 2,500 X10Ds for over $52 million, the largest single-vendor small drone order in Army history. Spain awarded a contract worth up to €18 million (about $18.7 million) for the drone in February 2025, and Norway followed with an initial tender worth 101 million Norwegian kroner (about $9.4 million) in July 2025.
The UK Ministry of Defence already has experience with Skydio. In May 2022, Defence Equipment and Support’s Future Capabilities Group awarded a contract worth about £3 million (about $3.8 million) for the company’s earlier X2D drone, delivered with British partner Marlborough Communications, after buying and testing 90 Skydio drones in 2020.

articles.title: Intl. conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid set for November
articles.body:
Intl. conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid set for November
TEHRAN – The 5th International conference on Global Coalition against Scientific Apartheid is planned to be held on November 10 in Tehran to promote justice in science and technology in the new world order, and honor the scientists martyred during the US-Israeli war against the country.
Organized by the World Islamic Peace Forum and Islamic Azad University, the key objectives of the conference involve promoting scientific justice as a prerequisite for global peace and justice, examining the state of scientific justice within the current and future global order, identifying instances of scientific apartheid, analyzing the assassination of scientists and the imposition of technological sanctions, and fostering coalitions among experts and scientific institutions worldwide.
The conference is centered around five main topics, including intellectual and philosophical foundations of scientific justice and overcoming science and technology apartheid; unilateralism, scientific and technological hegemony, and the future of world order; examples of scientific and technological apartheid and countermeasures; scientific justice, fair peace and development; as well as global coalition for justice in science and technology: from discourse to action.
Sanctions contradict UNESCO’s Open Access Policy
In April, Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf condemned sanctions imposed on the country’s science sector, saying that the sanctions are in opposition to UNESCO’s Open Access Policy.
Addressing the Global Ministerial Dialogue on Science Diplomacy, which was held at UNESCO Headquarters, Paris, France, on March 25 and 26, the minister said that as per Resolution 2231 of the Security Council, imposing sanctions on scientific activities has no legal validity, IRNA reported.
The two-day event was held under the theme ‘Science Diplomacy in a Rapidly Changing World: Building Peace in the Minds of Men and Women’.
Simaei-Sarraf delineated Iran’s viewpoints and perspectives on issues such as modern science diplomacy to address the challenges of the 21st century, the role of science diplomacy in safeguarding the security of science and promoting open access in scientific research, and the role of science diplomacy in fostering fair cooperation for the development and responsible use of new and emerging technologies.
On the sidelines of the event, the official held meetings with the Deputy Director-General, Xing Qu; Assistant Director-General for Natural Science, Lidia Arthur Brito; Assistant Director-General for Education, Stefania Giannini; and Assistant Director-General for External Relations of UNESCO, Firmin Edouard Matoko.
Moreover, Simaei-Sarraf held meetings with the ministers of science of Sri Lanka and Colombia and the deputy science ministers of Iraq and Switzerland.
In a meeting with Iranian professors residing in France and Germany, Simaei-Sarraf invited them to help enhance collaborations with the country.
The official also highlighted the need to amend laws and eliminate existing gaps to be able to benefit from the scientific capacities of Iranians living abroad. It was decided that 20 prominent Iranian professors residing in Europe would travel to Iran this summer to deliver speeches and hold scientific and educational workshops in different fields such as artificial intelligence, and renewable energy.
The Global Ministerial Dialogue on science diplomacy, as part of the International Decade of Sciences for Sustainable Development, aims to advance international dialogue on creating a new global framework for science diplomacy that addresses the current needs of society.
The dialogue aims to foster a high-level commitment to science diplomacy as an instrument for promoting dialogue and peace; explore innovative science diplomacy initiatives through exchanges between ministers, scientists, diplomats, and experts to contribute to peacebuilding and human rights protection; agree on a common framework to advance shared goals through science diplomacy; and highlight ongoing initiatives and opportunities in science diplomacy.

articles.title: US lawmakers plot to derail Trump’s Russian diesel deal
articles.body:
US lawmakers plot to derail Trump’s Russian diesel deal
A number of American lawmakers intend to block the Trump administration’s deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel through April and are threatening action against US companies involved in the trade. The bipartisan group is also planning to block the US Treasury from issuing such a waiver in the future.
US President Donald Trump announced the deal earlier this month, as US diesel prices hit a record $6.50+ per gallon in September and prices in parts of California topped $8. Under the waiver, struck just weeks ahead of the impending November midterm elections, Moscow agreed to immediately put 300,000 tons of diesel into the market, and commit to further releases.
The disruption of global energy markets, caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict, has resulted in rising gas prices in the US, further denting the positions of Republicans ahead of the vote. Diesel is the key fuel type extensively used in agriculture and freight; its price affects the cost of virtually all goods, resulting in further cost-of-living issues. Rural communities, smalltime farmers, and truckers are particularly vulnerable to diesel prices spikes.
Senate Democrats are now seeking to investigate the diesel deal, the Washington Post reported on Thursday, citing an unnamed Senate Democratic aide. According to the aide, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has requested companies involved in the scheme to preserve documents ahead of a possible probe by the panel.
“[The companies] should have liability concerns as well as investigative concerns,” the aide told WaPo.
Further action against the diesel deal has been taken by Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1), an outspoken hawk, Ukraine backer, and proponent of sanctions against Russia. The proposed legislation, titled the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, would effectively block Russian oil imports for good.
The bill would nullify the standing Russian oil waiver, “immediately rendering General License 135 ineffective and prohibiting future waivers or general licenses authorizing the importation of Russian energy products,” as well as strip the Treasury from the ability to expend funds “on agreements that violate the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022,” the legislation that sanctioned Russian energy products, including diesel, in the first place.
Apart from the energy part, the bill also would “reinforce critical intelligence support for Ukraine,” obliging spy agencies to cooperate with Kiev and to “notify congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.”

articles.title: Reuters: US sought to activate Starlink in Iran after strikes
articles.body:
Reuters: US sought to activate Starlink in Iran after strikes
TEHRAN – Successive US administrations have repeatedly asked SpaceX to activate or disable its Starlink satellite internet service in different countries to advance Washington’s foreign policy objectives, including requests to provide internet access inside Iran following US-Israeli strikes, Reuters reported on Saturday, citing six former senior US officials familiar with the matter.
According to the report, the administration of former US President Joe Biden asked SpaceX to activate Starlink in Iran during protests in September 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini. A former senior official in President Donald Trump’s administration and another person familiar with the matter told Reuters that the administration also discussed activating Starlink in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in June 2025 and February 2026, with the stated aim of expanding internet access and communications for anti-government protesters.
The report said neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX had publicly confirmed whether the terminals involved in the latest discussions were activated. It also cited a February report by The Wall Street Journal that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran.
The revelations come as Iran has formally protested the unauthorized operation of Starlink terminals on its territory, accusing Norway of failing to take effective action and raising concerns about the use of foreign satellite communications infrastructure by the United States and Israel.
Iran protests Norway’s inaction over Starlink
On October 4, Iran’s Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador to Tehran Paul Bjornstad to convey Tehran’s formal protest over the continued operation of unauthorized Starlink terminals inside Iran.
According to Iran’s Foreign Ministry, Mohammad Hassan-Nejad Pirkoohi, the ministry’s director general for international peace and security, told the Norwegian envoy that the United States and Israel were exploiting Starlink’s satellite communications infrastructure to pursue interventionist activities against Iran.
The Iranian official criticized Norway for failing to fulfill its responsibilities as one of the administrations involved in registering the Starlink network with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). He called on Oslo to take immediate and effective measures to halt unauthorized transmissions within Iranian territory and handed the ambassador a formal note of protest.
According to Tehran Times, the dispute had been under consideration by the ITU’s Radio Regulations Board since 2023. According to documents published by the international telecommunications body, Iran has repeatedly reported unauthorized Starlink operations within its territory.
The board has repeatedly called on Norway and the United States to take appropriate action to stop unauthorized transmissions, including by having the satellite operator remotely disable terminals operating without permission where necessary.
At its 98th meeting, the board concluded that there was evidence of unauthorized Starlink transmissions inside Iran and urged Norway to take measures within its capacity to stop them. It also asked Norway and the United States to explain why terminals operating without authorization in Iran could not be disabled in the same way as terminals in several other countries.
At its 101st meeting, the board concluded that Norway’s actions did not comply with relevant ITU resolutions and Article 18 of the Radio Regulations. However, it said it lacked the authority to suspend frequency assignments to satellite systems on the grounds that the administration responsible for notifying the network had failed to comply with the rules.
Tehran has maintained that the continued operation of Starlink terminals without authorization violates Iran’s sovereignty and national security. The dispute also highlights questions over the responsibilities of governments involved in registering satellite networks and the ability of operators to prevent services from being provided in countries where they are not authorized.
Starlink and US foreign policy
Reuters reported that the Biden administration also asked SpaceX to disable terminals allegedly used by Yemen’s Houthi movement and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Former US officials said the administration shared intelligence with the company concerning the possible use of diverted Starlink terminals by the two groups and requested that the devices be identified and deactivated. At least some terminals were subsequently switched off, according to two of the officials.
The disclosures have renewed questions about the extent to which US administrations rely on Elon Musk’s privately owned company to implement foreign policy and security objectives. SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the reported requests concerning Iran.
For Tehran, the issue extends beyond internet access to the regulation of satellite communications and the use of foreign technology inside Iranian territory without authorization. Iranian officials have repeatedly called on the countries responsible for the Starlink network’s registration, as well as its operator, to ensure that the service complies with international telecommunications regulations and Iran’s requirement for authorization.

articles.title: Saudi strikes kill 11 in Yemen as Houthi missiles target Saudi cities
articles.body:
Saudi strikes kill 11 in Yemen as Houthi missiles target Saudi cities
Houthi media reported a series of ‘Saudi enemy air strikes’ targeting Sanaa, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two missiles
Houthi media reported that Saudi strikes killed 11 people in Yemeni capital Sanaa on Saturday, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities.
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of “Saudi enemy air strikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others.
A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said.
Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region.

articles.title: Russia launches new stealth corvette Grozny
articles.body:
- Russia’s Amur Shipbuilding Plant launched the Project 20380 corvette Grozny for the Pacific Fleet on Oct. 23 in Komsomolsk-on-Amur.
- It is the fifth ship of the class built at the plant, laid down in August 2021, with commissioning expected within the next few years.
Russia’s Amur Shipbuilding Plant has launched the multipurpose corvette Grozny, the fifth Project 20380 warship it has built for the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet, the fleet’s press service said. The ceremony took place on Oct. 23 in Komsomolsk-on-Amur, in Russia’s Far East, more than five years after the ship was laid down on Aug. 23, 2021.
The corvette was rolled out of the construction hall and floated with the help of the Amurets launch pontoon dock, then moved to a pier where workers will finish outfitting it. Russian officials did not give a date for its commissioning, saying only that the ship is expected to join the fleet within the next few years.
“The crew for the corvette Grozny has been formed and began training on October 5, after which it will arrive at the plant to complete the ship together with you and bring it into the fleet in the coming years,” said Adm. Viktor Liina, commander of the Pacific Fleet, RIA Novosti reported.
Project 20380, known in the West as the Steregushchiy class, was designed by the Almaz Central Marine Design Bureau and was the first major surface combatant class developed in Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The ships use stealth shaping to reduce their radar signature. The standard design displaces about 2,200 tonnes fully loaded, is about 104 m (341 feet) long and is armed with a 100 mm gun, Redut surface-to-air missiles, Uran anti-ship missiles, close-in weapon systems and anti-submarine torpedoes, and carries a helicopter. Officials did not detail Grozny’s specific equipment.
Four ships of the class already serve with the Pacific Fleet, all built at the Amur plant: Sovershenny, Gromky, Geroy Rossiyskoy Federatsii Aldar Tsydenzhapov and Rezky. Officers have said the corvettes have proven able to operate as far as the Indian Ocean.
The plant, part of the state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation, is the Pacific Fleet’s main source of new warships in the Far East. It is currently building 10 ships of various projects, and its order book is fully covered by state defense contracts, according to Khabarovsk Krai Governor Dmitry Demeshin, who said the yard has delivered 99 submarines and more than 100 surface ships to the Pacific Fleet over its history.

articles.title: Israel needs sanctions-proof economy – Netanyahu
articles.body:
Israel needs sanctions-proof economy – Netanyahu
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said his country must prepare to adapt its economy to global sanctions, citing declining international support and a potential end to US financial and military aid.
Public opinion toward Israel has grown increasingly negative amid the wars in Gaza and Iran. In the US, a recent Chicago Council on Global Affairs report recorded the country’s lowest favorability rating since its polling began in 1978, with a majority supporting reducing or ending military aid.
Last month, the UK announced a ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband describing settlers as “terrorists” supported by Netanyahu’s government and accusing them of ethnically cleansing Palestinians. The same day, 11 other countries, including France, Spain, and Canada, joined Britain in a statement supporting the two-state solution and announcing plans to impose or consider restrictions on trade with the settlements.
“We must understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions,” Netanyahu said in an interview which aired on Israel’s Channel 10 on Friday.
“We need to prepare an alternative economy capable of functioning by circumventing these sanctions,” he added, noting that blockchain technology, which underpins cryptocurrencies, was among the options under consideration and that he had already requested an implementation plan.
The Israeli prime minister also expressed concern over a potential shift in Washington’s position, saying that “it’s only a matter of time” before US military aid is completely “over.”
“If you think we’re going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that’s tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won’t happen because America has changed,” he said.
Under an agreement signed in 2016, Washington committed to providing $38 billion in military aid through 2028. Netanyahu previously said he wanted to phase out the financial component of US military assistance within ten years.
Former prime minister and opposition figure Yair Lapid seized on the remarks, saying that “Netanyahu now admits, in his own words, that if his government is returned to power, American military aid will end and Israel will face sanctions that will devastate our economy, trigger uncontrolled price surges, and cause irreparable damage.”
The comments come days before Israel’s first national election since the October 7 Hamas attacks, with accountability for security failures, the cost of living, ultra-Orthodox military service, and the country’s international standing among the issues facing voters. Neither Netanyahu’s allies nor the opposition have a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

articles.title: Mass protests grip Western Europe (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Mass protests grip Western Europe (VIDEOS)
Mass protests have swept across Europe over the weekend, with demonstrators clashing with riot police amid widespread anger over soaring living costs and government policies.
The unrest has largely been inspired by the protests in France, which began in September. Spearheaded by students, they were originally aimed at rising education costs, a lack of teachers, and the poor condition of educational facilities. They eventually morphed into widespread violence and now carry a broader anti-government undertone.
France remains the hotbed of the protests, with at least 410,000 people hitting the streets nationwide on Saturday, including some 110,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. The CGT union, one of the key organizers of the demonstrations, put the estimate nearly twice as high, at about 800,000.

articles.title: Sudan legal amendment puts journalists at risk of death penalty
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Journalists, politicians face death penalty under Sudan legal amendment, activists warn
A recent amendment to Sudan's 1991 criminal code could mean that journalists and politicians could now face the death penalty for online posts, rights groups and activists have warned.
The amendment now includes media publications and electronic media as potential crimes against the state.
The development comes amid an armed conflict between the Sudanese forces and the notorious RSF paramilitary group, which has raged on since 2023 and significantly hindered freedom of expression and journalism in the country.
It also comes at the same time the government implemented a mechanism designed to tackle cybercrime. However, activists state this has been used to monitor publications, media outlets and potential dissidents.
Sudanese journalist Majid Mohammed told The New Arab that the increasing punishment for those who publish content online is inconsistent with the government’s stated goal of opening and improving dialogue with citizens in the country.
“The amendments have failed to distinguish between the freedom of Sudanese people and enemies in Sudan who may use social media or online platforms to harm the state,” he said.
He urged a “review of the amendments, because their implementation will create and directly lead to the end of any dialogue initiatives and will create a negative climate for any consensus and agreements".
He also noted one of his biggest concerns was it would prevent the press from fulfilling its role towards the nation and civilians, and from assisting state institutions from carrying out their responsibilities through monitoring, oversight, and combating misinformation.
Amendment to penal code
Earlier this week, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the commander-in-chief of the Sudanese Armed Forces, issued a temporary decree under the Miscellaneous Amendments Act of 2026, which included changes to several laws.
The amendments were published in a special supplement to the Official Gazette.
Article 51, which pertains to inciting war against the state and includes terms such as the training of individuals, collecting weapons, or attempting to support or incite such actions, was amended to include electronic and media publications.
The original article states that anyone charged with the aforementioned “shall be considered to have committed the crime of inciting war against the state and shall be punished by death or a lesser term of life imprisonment, with the possibility of confiscating all their assets”.
Backlash against the amendment
According to local media reports, the amendments have sparked backlash among journalists, activists and politicians, and since the change, there has been a marked decrease in discussions, posts and articles on social media from Sudan.
Some activists have decried the move, stating that the government will likely exploit the amendment, and interpret any dissent or expressions of opinion as a crime against the state under the penal code.
The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate announced in a statement on Friday that it stood firm in its rejection of the amendment to Article 51 of the 1991 Criminal Code, and Prime Minister Kamil Idris’ decision to establish the National Mechanism for Combatting Cybercrime.
The syndicate said there would be serious repercussions to the measures, and press freedoms, and the right to access certain information, particularly in light of the ongoing war, would be severely hindered.
It cautioned against granting further powers for the state to monitor and track media outlets and social media platforms, or act against publishers based on vague descriptions and the wording of the penal code.
The political group The Radical Change Alliance also this week rejected the amendments, demanding that the changes be repealed and calling for an end to the prosecution of journalists and activists.
Human rights activist Othman Saleh told The New Arab that “the intention behind this amendment is clear – it's to restrict freedom of publication, expression and press. It also hinders the work of activists and journalists who document violations from all sides, and analyse and express opinions on all issues”.

articles.title: The West’s double standard on global unrest
articles.body:
The West’s double standard on global unrest
Ideology, strategic interests and cultural ignorance explain why protests in Hong Kong and beyond are viewed through a selective lens
In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play.
Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants.
A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.”

articles.title: Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, intelligence memo warns
articles.body:
Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, intelligence memo warns
- US intelligence says Iran has stepped up efforts to target US personnel, and “lethal plotting” against American citizens is at “advanced stages”, according to a memo from Jay Clayton.
- The warning came after the US cut staffing at its Saudi Arabia mission and updated travel advice for more than a dozen Gulf and Middle East countries because of rising Houthi threats.
- The wider Iran war is now nearing nine months and is adding pressure on President Donald Trump, with the conflict and regional attacks affecting US security and politics.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached “advanced stages”, a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters.
The alert from director of national intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces.
Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with a rise in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory.
“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel,” Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated Oct 23.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” he added.
CIA director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios.
The State Department on Oct 21 ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
On Oct 24, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis.
“When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” a US official said.
“The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region,” the official said.
The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission.
The Iran war is a week away from entering its ninth month and has significantly weighed on the approval ratings of US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections on Nov 3. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping and entertainment complex in the Russian city of Belgorod during a mass drone attack overnight on 25 October, when the mall was closed and no visitors were inside, according to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Russian authorities reported that a civilian was killed and 10 people were injured in the broader mass drone attack on Belgorod. One of the injured was an ambulance worker, according to the regional operational headquarters.
The majority of the drones reportedly targeted one area in the city center, according to ASTRA.
Belgorod’s largest shopping complex targeted
Exilenova+ identified the reported target as MegaGRINN, Belgorod’s largest shopping and entertainment complex covering about 163,000 square meters. The facility houses more than 200 stores, a supermarket, restaurants, a cinema, and entertainment areas.
Belgorod is a Russian city about 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine’s northeastern border and roughly 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. The city and surrounding oblast have repeatedly come under Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
Belgorod Oblast borders Ukraine’s Sumy, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts. Russian forces have used the region to launch missile and drone attacks on Ukraine and to stage ground offensives across the border.
Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian retail infrastructure
The reported strike comes amid an intensified Russian campaign against Ukrainian retail and logistics infrastructure. These attacks have included strikes on shopping centers during business hours, including a 21 August Russian drone attack on the crowded Soniachna Halereia mall in Kryvyi Rih, where 16 people were killed and more than 120 injured.
The reported strike on MegaGRINN took place overnight, when the complex was reportedly closed and empty of visitors. Russian authorities reported casualties from the wider attack on Belgorod, but have not linked them to the mall.

articles.title: Democrats ready to sacrifice Americans’ well-being for ideology – guests to RT (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Democrats ready to sacrifice Americans’ well-being for ideology – guests to RT (VIDEOS)
Democrats’ vehement opposition to the diesel deal that US President Donald Trump struck with Russia earlier this month proves they do not care about Americans’ well-being, guests have told RT.
According to recent media reports, a group of Senate Democrats are working on ways to block the arrangement that is meant to rein in skyrocketing diesel prices in the US, while a Republican Russia hawk has put forward legislation to nullify Trump’s efforts.
Speaking to RT on Saturday, American journalist John Varoli said that Democrats are engaged in a “political witch hunt” and so have no qualms about targeting a deal that is “in the interest of the American people.”
He predicted that should Democrats prevail in next month’s midterm elections, they would do “everything possible just to ruin this deal and to inhibit it” for purely ideological reasons.
American broadcaster Garland Nixon concurred that driven by “ideological anger at Russia,” Democrats are showing a disregard for the plight of American consumers.
“At this point, what we’re seeing [is that Democrats] are totally ignoring domestic issues, domestic policy, totally ignoring the working class, and they’re focusing only on foreign policy,” Nixon told RT.
He warned that if left unchecked, rising fuel prices could plunge the US economy into a “severe recession.”
Legal and media analyst Lionel told RT that opinion polls that predict a Democratic victory in the midterms should be taken with a grain of salt. He argued that American voters could punish the party for its efforts to undermine the diesel deal.
“This is political suicide to proceed with this,” he added.
Matt Weinglass, producer, director and host of The Homeless Left, argued that opposition to the diesel deal is driven by a decade-long political narrative vilifying Trump, which has taken precedence over the economic interests of ordinary Americans.
“It’s not going to help the American people. It’s going to help the billionaire class and the donor class, the people that have wanted to keep this conflict alive as long as possible,” Weinglass told RT. He also suggested that European leaders could join forces with Trump’s domestic opponents ahead of the midterms.
Former Democratic Congressman Dennis Kucinich argued that his former colleagues should abandon their longstanding hostility toward Russia and focus instead on ending the Ukraine conflict and the war with Iran, both of which have disrupted global energy markets and driven up fuel prices for ordinary Americans.
“There’s this animosity that has built up. And some Democrats are just having trouble letting it go, and they seize on every opportunity,” he told RT, dismissing the proposed legislation to block Russian fuel imports as “going nowhere.”
Rather than trying to derail Trump’s diesel deal, Kucinich urged Washington to redirect its resources toward domestic priorities. “We have problems here in America to take care of health care, retirement security, education, on and on and on,” he said. “That’s what we’ve got to be focused on, not on war.”
Since diesel is extensively used in agriculture and freight, its price has a direct impact on the cost of numerous other goods. Farmers and truckers are particularly vulnerable to diesel price spikes.
Amid global energy supply chain disruptions caused by the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran, as well as the Ukraine conflict, diesel prices have risen considerably in the US, hitting a record $6.50+ per gallon in September, with prices in parts of California topping $8 per gallon.
The soaring costs have become an increasingly pressing domestic issue for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Earlier this month, the US president stated that Washington and Moscow had struck a deal for Russia to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially another three million tons. Shortly afterward, the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing the fuel to be sold, delivered, and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.

articles.title: Opposition leader says Netanyahu ‘no longer fit’ to lead Israel
articles.body:
Just days before pivotal Israeli elections, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot said Saturday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is “no longer fit” to lead the country, warning that his economic plan to counter potential international sanctions threatens national security, Anadolu reports.
On US social media company X, the Yashar party leader accused Netanyahu of turning his attention to “dismantling the Israeli economy for generations ahead” after “dismantling Israeli society and weakening the army.”
Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s recent remarks are “conclusive proof that he has lost touch with reality and moved into a world of delusions,” accusing him of proposing preparations to disconnect from the global financial system in response to Israel’s declining international standing.
“This is the madness of a man who is no longer fit to lead the country,” he said.
His comments came one day after Netanyahu said he had requested an economic plan involving alternative payment methods, including cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology, in preparation for possible international economic and banking sanctions.
Netanyahu expressed concern about potential sanctions, including restrictions on the Israeli banking system.
Netanyahu did not say Israel would withdraw from the global economic system. The characterization of the proposal as economic isolation formed part of Eisenkot’s criticism.
Netanyahu also warned that US military aid would not last forever, urging Israel to prepare for its possible end and to strengthen military self-reliance.
– Warning against economic isolation
Eisenkot mocked the proposal as “Bibicoin,” combining Netanyahu’s nickname, Bibi, with his proposed use of alternative payment methods and financial technologies.
He questioned how Israeli technology companies serving foreign clients would receive payments or attract overseas investment if they had to bypass international banking and rely on cryptocurrencies.
He also questioned how international acquisitions of Israeli companies could proceed if the economy moved toward isolation from the global financial system.
He warned that this course could prompt Israeli companies to relocate abroad, cause losses in savings and investments, and encourage citizens to leave the country.
Eisenkot said the consequences could include fewer jobs and reduced resources for healthcare and education, ultimately harming national security.
“This is not an imagined nightmare scenario, but Netanyahu’s plan for Israel if he is reelected” on Tuesday, he said.
“This is a real warning. Israel will not withstand another four years like these.”
-Controversial remarks
Netanyahu’s remarks also drew criticism in Israeli political and economic circles.
Israeli media cited an unnamed senior economic official who said that using cryptocurrencies and alternative financial technologies to circumvent banking sanctions would not achieve the intended goal. The official warned that merely proposing such an approach could damage the economy.
The debate comes amid mounting international pressure on Israel for its war on the Gaza Strip, settlement expansion, and occupier attacks in the occupied West Bank.
The UK and other Western countries have taken measures against individuals and entities linked to Israeli settlements, while concerns have grown in Israel about broader economic and diplomatic pressure.
The exchanges also come ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections, in which Netanyahu and Eisenkot are competing to lead the next government.
In his post, Eisenkot urged Israelis to vote for “a better shared future.”
The former military chief is one of Netanyahu’s leading rivals, with the two sharply divided on security and economic policies, the country’s leadership, and its foreign relations.
Israeli politics also remains deeply divided on responsibility for the failures surrounding the October 2023 attack, the conduct of subsequent wars, military conscription, the economy, and relations with the US and other Western countries.

articles.title: Tehran, Bangkok underline enhancing co-op in ICT
articles.body:
Tehran, Bangkok underline enhancing co-op in ICT
TEHRAN – Iranian and Thai officials have highlighted the importance of expanding joint efforts in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector, boosting regional and international interactions, and developing a memorandum of understanding between the two sides.
Deputy ICT minister, Mohammad-Hafez Hakami, and Thai ambassador to Iran, Sake Nopthaisong, met on Tuesday, IRNA reported.
Highlighting the longstanding partnership between Iran and Thailand, Nopthaisong called for continued cooperation between the two countries.
The official went on to say that since he was appointed Thai ambassador to Tehran, he has been interested in getting familiar with Iran’s accomplishments and capacities in different fields like artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and emerging technologies.
For his part, Hakami said that since the Asia-Pacific Telecommunity (APT) headquarters is in Bangkok, Thailand plays a significant role in strengthening regional technological cooperation. He suggested benefiting from the capacities of the two nations to develop interactions.
The two sides underscored the need to draft and sign a memorandum of understanding to foster bilateral relations and technological cooperation.
GII 2026 places Tehran 65th among top 100 science and technology clusters
The Global Innovation Index (GII) has ranked Tehran as the world’s 65th-largest science and technology (S&T) cluster this year, according to a report released by the UN’s World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
Each year, the GII identifies and ranks the world’s top 100 innovation clusters. Using a bottom-up, data-driven approach that transcends administrative and political boundaries, the GII identifies geographic areas with a high concentration of inventors, scientific authors, and venture capital (VC) activity. These innovation clusters often extend across multiple municipalities or subnational regions and, in some cases, span two or more countries.
Three metrics determine the top 100: the locations of inventors listed in patent applications filed under the WIPO Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), the affiliations of authors of published scientific articles, and the locations of companies receiving venture capital funding.
The GII 2026, under the theme “Powering entrepreneurs at the frontier of science”, examines how scientific breakthroughs become deep science startups and spinouts.
In addition to China and India, six other middle-income economies have clusters among the top 100, including Brazil (1 cluster), the Islamic Republic of Iran (1), Egypt (1), Malaysia (2), Mexico (1), and Turkey (1).
Tehran is the only cluster within Iran that falls within the top 100 innovation clusters in 2026. In 2026, Tehran had 405 PCT applications, 58,732 scientific publications, 107 venture capital deals, 0.0 percent Share of global PCT applications, 0.7 percent share of global scientific publications, and 0.0 percent share of global venture capital deals, making it the 65th largest innovation cluster and 88 innovation cluster by intensity, slipping down from 63rd and 85th, respectively in 2025.
The city’s estimated cluster population, PCT application per capita, and scientific publication capita amount to 7,852,733; 52; and 7,497 respectively, IRNA reported.
The venture capital pre-deals per capita is about 14, and the total innovation intensity share per capita is 0.097.
In patent registration, medical technology ranked first (with 19 percent share), followed by computer technology, civil engineering, and pharmaceuticals.
Top publishing organizations in Tehran are University of Tehran with 5,232 articles, Islamic Azad University with 4,081 articles, and Iran University of Science and Technology with 3,725 articles. A majority of published articles are in engineering fields.
In a recent global ranking by StartupBlink 2026, Tehran’s position has advanced by 20 spots, ranking 348 among the world’s most innovative cities.
Tehran is home to 96 startups, making up 81 percent of all startups in the country. Tehran has approximately 1 startup per 100,000 people. In 2025, the ecosystem recorded an annual growth rate of over 36 percent. The city is currently ranked as the 1st strongest startup ecosystem in Iran, having remained stable since 2025. At the regional level, Tehran ranks 11th in West Asia, having moved up 2 spots since 2025.
According to Iran Innovation Zone, the achievement is the result of strengthening innovation infrastructure and developing interactions among different sectors operating in the knowledge-based economy, Mehr news agency reported.
The report by StartupBlink has highlighted the role of Pardis Technology Park, the country’s largest technology and innovation hub, as one of the driving forces of Iran’s knowledge-based economy. The park hosts hundreds of knowledge-based and technology companies, creating business development infrastructure and providing a platform for enhancing cooperation among startups, investors, large industries, and institutions.
Moreover, hosting the International Innovation and Technology Exhibition (INOTEX) every year, Pardis Technology Park plays a key role in networking and connecting experts in the innovation ecosystem. According to the report, thanks to the capacities of Pardis Technology Parks, Iran’s startup ecosystem ranks 95 globally.
The Innovation and Prosperity Fund and MCI (Hamrah Aval – Iran’s first mobile operator) Ventures are the two other key agents that have developed Iran’s innovation ecosystem by facilitating the growth of technology and knowledge-based companies.
Iran ranks 58th globally in ‘Corporate Engagement’, an indicator that reflects the effective interactions between large industries and innovative and technological companies.
Fintech, the leading industry in Iran, ranks 72nd globally, 5th in the Middle East, indicating the country’s high capacity in the development of financial technologies. Iran Fintech Industry has 23 startups, representing 19 percent of all startups in Iran.
In the Global Startup Ecosystem Index 2026, Iran’s startup ecosystem is ranked 103 worldwide, holding steady compared to the previous year. The Iranian startup ecosystem ranks 10th in West Asia, having remained stable since 2025. It ranks right after Oman and is followed by Iraq.
The country has 118 startups, representing one percent of all startups in the Middle East. This equals approximately one startup per 100,000 people. The ecosystem grew by +54.4 percent over the past year.

articles.title: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA
articles.body:
Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA: "Now is the time"
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with the CIA, the latest ploy in the growing efforts from the Trump administration to remove Cuba's communist regime from power.
"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio wrote Friday on X. "The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."
Shortly afterward, the CIA reposted Rubio's message and a similar call in Spanish for Cubans to work with the agency. A video was posted alongside the message showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.
A strict U.S. embargo and sanctions seeking to put pressure on Cuba's communist government have led to prices of basic goods skyrocketing and decreased access to medical care for its citizens. Cubans reported waiting in bread lines for hours and others reported lining up to see a doctor.
Last week, the U.S. government announced additional economic sanctions on Cuba's state-run bank, saying the institution had ties to Iran.
President Trump said on Friday during a campaign rally in South Florida that "we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran." He was referring to the U.S. Navy warships deployed near the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr. Trump added: "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Cuba's government has pushed back, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla responding Friday on X, saying: "We reject any threats stemming from U.S. ambitions toward Cuba."
Rodriguez Parrilla added: "Our shores are lined with beautiful beaches, but they are also rugged and inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile intentions and a desire for domination."

articles.title: flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
articles.body:
flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
biodegradable capsules packed with native seeds and beneficial fungi help restore wildfire-damaged landscapes across northern quebec.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
flash forest plants for life after wildfires
Across the blackened forests of northern Quebec, drones fly above the remains of burned trees, launching small, seed-filled capsules into the earth. Each carries the beginnings of a new tree, packed with ingredients intended to help it grow in damaged soil. The system is developed by Canadian company Flash Forest, which is using aerial technology to replant landscapes devastated by wildfire, including remote areas that are difficult to reach on foot.
The work follows Quebec’s devastating 2023 wildfire season, when around 4.5 million hectares of forest burned across the province. Flash Forest has since expanded its planting operations across Canada. According to its latest impact report, the company planted 686,147 trees across five sites in 2025, covering 429 hectares of burned forest. The technology allows large areas to be seeded quickly while keeping heavy planting equipment off the forest floor.
tiny engineered pods give seeds a place to grow
At the center of Flash Forest’s operation is a biodegradable seed pod designed to support a young tree through its earliest stages of growth. Each capsule contains nutrients, moisture-retaining additives and mycorrhizal fungi, which can help developing roots absorb nutrients from the soil. Customized drones propel the pods directly into the ground, where the seeds can germinate without first spending years growing in a nursery.
The capsules are manufactured to consistent dimensions so they can pass through the drones’ automated feeding mechanisms. Their composition is developed around the needs of the seeds, with materials intended to retain moisture and support early growth. By sowing seeds directly into the landscape, the company also avoids the transplant shock that can affect nursery-grown saplings. Yet even with this engineered starting point, germination remains dependent on the conditions of each planting site.
collecting millions of seeds in northern quebec
Behind the automated planting process is a remarkable effort to gather seeds from the forests themselves. Flash Forest has been working with the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation to restore areas damaged by the 2023 wildfires, which destroyed wildlife habitats and affected traditional hunting grounds. When northern Quebec faced a shortage of native seeds, the team worked with local partners to collect jack pine cones directly from trees, traveling by snowmobile and climbing through forests in temperatures as low as -30°C.
The winter operation yielded approximately 8.5 million jack pine seeds, which were incorporated into planting pods within five months of collection. For Benny Blacksmith of the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation, the aerial process offers a way to restore habitats while avoiding further disturbance to the land. He describes the impact of the fires on wildlife, recalling how even small animals disappeared from affected areas, disrupting the food sources of larger species. The community hopes to see native trees such as white birch and black spruce return to the damaged landscape.
the longer process of rebuilding a forest
Flash Forest’s work continues after the drones have finished planting. The company surveys each site to assess existing vegetation before returning to monitor seedling growth. Experimental plots compare the performance of its engineered pods against untreated seeds and areas left to regenerate naturally. Some sites in Quebec have already experienced delayed germination following warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall, with further monitoring planned for fall 2026.
Wildfire is itself part of the natural cycle of boreal forests. Jack pine cones can open in response to heat, releasing seeds onto the exposed ground, although increasingly severe fires and changing climate conditions can interrupt this process. Flash Forest’s technology offers a way to introduce new seeds where that recovery is struggling. The drones can put them into the ground in a matter of seconds. Whether they establish themselves, and what kind of forest eventually grows around them, will become apparent over the years ahead.

articles.title: Iran says resumption of war would not change its stances
articles.body:
AP Photo
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct. 25 that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country’s positions.
“Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same,” said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
The remarks come amid mounting U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Oct. 23 that Washington “may do another little Epic Fury,” referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on Feb. 28.
“They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past,” the Iranian top diplomat said.
“The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same,” said Araghchi.
“To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces.”
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
At the same time, Washington is reinforcing its military presence in the region. Two U.S. aircraft carrier strike groups are operating in the Middle East, a third is approaching from the Pacific, and an amphibious assault ship carrying Marines is also being deployed, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 24.
The buildup came as U.S. intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a memo on Oct. 23 that Iran had significantly increased efforts to target Americans.
Washington has also ordered diplomatic and military personnel to leave some locations as security concerns grow.
The administration is weighing its options ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, reports said, while warning that renewed strikes could trigger Iranian retaliation, put US forces at greater risk and push global energy prices higher.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorization, moves strongly opposed by Washington and 
countries in the region.

articles.title: Emotional struggles are linked to vulnerable narcissism but not grandiose narcissism, meta-analysis finds
articles.body:
A new statistical review of data from more than 12,000 adults suggests that difficulties with managing emotions are moderately linked to one specific form of narcissism, while showing virtually no connection to another. The research, published in Personality and Individual Differences, indicates that people with insecure and defensive narcissistic traits tend to struggle with emotional control, whereas those with more boastful, dominant narcissistic traits generally do not report these same struggles. These findings help clarify why past studies on narcissism and emotional health have produced conflicting results, and they may point to specific emotional skills that could be targeted in therapy.
In psychology, trait narcissism refers to a persistent pattern of personality characteristics centered on interpersonal antagonism, which includes feeling entitled, manipulating others, and lacking empathy. Rather than being a single uniform trait, narcissism is generally divided into two main subtypes: grandiose and vulnerable. Grandiose narcissism matches the common stereotype of a narcissist, featuring an outgoing, dominant, attention-seeking, and aggressively self-confident style. Vulnerable narcissism, while sharing the same core of entitlement and self-centeredness, looks very different on the surface, involving introversion, fragile self-esteem, deep feelings of inadequacy, and a heightened sensitivity to rejection.
Both forms of narcissism are associated with problems in relationships, including a lack of care for a partner’s distress, relationship dissatisfaction, and even intimate partner violence; a 2024 meta-analysis found that violence was more strongly tied to vulnerable narcissism (a correlation of 0.25) than to grandiose narcissism (0.11). Because personality traits themselves are deeply ingrained and difficult to change, psychologists often look for modifiable behaviors and skills that might help improve how narcissistic individuals function in daily life. One promising target is emotion dysregulation, which refers to difficulty understanding, managing, and responding to feelings in a healthy way that aligns with a person’s goals and social norms.
“Our broader interest in this area stems from wanting to understand the psychological factors that contribute to the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people with high levels of narcissism,” senior author Megan L. Willis, an associate professor in the School of Behavioural and Health Sciences and the Healthy Brain and Mind Research Centre at Australian Catholic University, told PsyPost. “I’m particularly interested in factors that may be modifiable – that is, things that we may be able to prevent or improve through psychological intervention.”
When psychologists study emotion dysregulation, they often look at several distinct areas where a person’s emotional control can break down. These areas include refusing to accept negative feelings, lacking awareness or clarity about what emotion is actually occurring, struggling to stay focused on tasks when upset, failing to control impulsive behaviors during distress, and lacking effective strategies to calm down. Studies linking narcissism to these emotional difficulties have produced confusing results, with some finding that narcissistic people had worse emotional control and others finding no link or even better emotional control.
Psychologists began to suspect that these contradictions happened because studies were measuring different subtypes of narcissism. For instance, a 2017 study of Chinese university students found that students with vulnerable narcissistic traits reported substantial trouble managing their emotions, while those with grandiose traits actually reported fewer emotional difficulties, which the authors linked to their higher self-esteem. Similarly, a 2020 study of undergraduates indicated that the defensive, self-protective side of narcissism was tied to poor emotion recognition and messy emotional reactions, whereas the assertive, self-promoting side was linked to better emotional management.
To make sense of the growing body of research, a 2024 systematic review summarized the existing literature and observed a consistent link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional struggles, alongside a lack of evidence connecting grandiose narcissism to those same struggles. However, that earlier review only summarized the studies qualitatively rather than mathematically combining their data, and it mixed psychiatric patients with the general public, which can weaken the correlations researchers observe. Willis, lead author Ria Tziliaskopoulos, and their colleagues at Australian Catholic University set out to conduct a full meta-analysis, a statistical technique that pools data from multiple studies to estimate the strength of the relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation in the general adult population.
“We wanted to establish the strength of the relationship between emotion dysregulation and narcissism in general, as well as determine whether this relationship differed between grandiose and vulnerable narcissism,” Willis explained.
The researchers searched five major academic databases through January 2026 to find studies written in English that measured both trait narcissism and emotion dysregulation in adults outside clinical settings. They excluded studies focusing on children or specialized groups like psychiatric patients or prison inmates, ensuring the results would reflect everyday adult populations. This screening process yielded 26 eligible studies from 25 reports, encompassing a combined total of 12,209 participants with average ages ranging from 18.7 to 62 years across countries including the United States, Italy, Turkey, China, Iran, and Brazil.
Because each included study used questionnaires to measure personality and emotional habits, the authors categorized the narcissism questionnaires into three groups: those measuring grandiose narcissism, those measuring vulnerable narcissism, and “combined” measures that blended both traits into a single score. For instance, the widely used Narcissistic Personality Inventory counted as a grandiose measure and the Hypersensitive Narcissism Scale as a vulnerable one, while the 2020 undergraduate study’s self-promoting “admiration” scale was counted as grandiose and its defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable.
Twenty-two of the 26 studies measured emotional difficulties using a standard questionnaire called the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale, which scores both overall dysregulation and the six specific problem areas like impulse control and emotional awareness. The researchers extracted 80 individual statistical correlations from the 26 studies and used a method called robust variance estimation to account for the fact that several studies contributed multiple data points from the same group of people.
In statistical terms, a correlation ranges from -1 to 1, where 0 means no relationship, positive values mean two traits tend to rise together, and negative values mean one tends to fall as the other rises. By common convention, values of about 0.10 to 0.29 are considered weak, 0.30 to 0.49 moderate, and 0.50 or above strong. When the researchers pooled all 80 data points together without separating the narcissism subtypes, they found a weak positive correlation of 0.15 between overall narcissism and emotion dysregulation. This meant that across the entire dataset, higher levels of narcissism were only slightly associated with greater trouble managing emotions.
When the team broke the data down by narcissism subtype, a sharp divide emerged that helps explain why the overall correlation was so small. Vulnerable narcissism showed a moderate positive correlation of 0.37 with emotion dysregulation across 11 studies. In contrast, grandiose narcissism showed a correlation of 0.04 across 21 studies, a number so close to zero that it was not statistically significant.
“The relationship with vulnerable narcissism was moderate in size, which is quite a meaningful relationship in individual differences research,” Willis noted. “Narcissism reflects a cluster of personality traits, so we wouldn’t expect any single psychological factor to explain it. The size of the relationship suggests that difficulties regulating emotions are an important part of the psychological profile of people high in vulnerable narcissism.”
Measures that combined both forms of narcissism fell right in the middle, showing a weak positive correlation of 0.25 across five studies. Follow-up statistical comparisons confirmed that the link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional difficulties was substantially stronger than the link for grandiose narcissism. The authors also checked whether a few debatable coding choices drove the results. Dropping the grandiose scale of the Pathological Narcissism Inventory, which critics say overlaps too much with vulnerable traits, left grandiose narcissism at 0.03, and dropping the one study that counted the defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable narcissism left vulnerable narcissism at 0.37.
“The findings may help explain some of the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people high in vulnerable narcissism,” Willis said. “They tend to be hypersensitive to rejection and criticism, and our findings suggest they are also more likely to have difficulty regulating their emotions. When they feel rejected or criticized, they may struggle to manage the emotions that arise in these situations. This could contribute to hostile or aggressive responses, which can create conflict and damage their relationships with others.”
The researchers then examined the four or five studies that reported scores for each of the six domains of emotional difficulty, pooling all types of narcissism together. They found weak but statistically reliable correlations with three specific problem areas: limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies had a correlation of 0.21, trouble controlling impulses when upset had a correlation of 0.19, and refusing to accept negative emotions had a correlation of 0.18. Meanwhile, narcissism was not statistically linked to lacking emotional awareness (which had a slight negative correlation of -0.08), lacking emotional clarity (0.13), or struggling to focus on goal-directed behaviors when distressed (0.13). The link with emotional awareness was weaker than the link with every other domain.
The authors suggest this pattern means the emotional struggles tied to narcissism may be less about failing to notice feelings and more about how a person reacts once an unpleasant emotion arrives, such as struggling to accept the feeling, acting impulsively, or feeling there is no healthy way to calm down. Because these analyses drew on only a handful of studies and combined all forms of narcissism, they cannot show whether the pattern differs between grandiose and vulnerable traits. The authors note that these specific breakdowns could help explain why people high in narcissism may lash out, blame others, or withdraw during relationship conflicts.
These results align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which also found that emotion dysregulation was tied to vulnerable rather than grandiose narcissism, although that earlier study tested psychiatric outpatients rather than the general adult samples analyzed in the new review.
The findings sit in partial tension with the 2020 study of undergraduates described earlier, which PsyPost covered in 2019, where the self-promoting side of grandiose narcissism was linked to fewer emotional difficulties and better emotional awareness. The meta-analysis included that study but counted its defensive rivalry scale as vulnerable narcissism, and across all the grandiose questionnaires combined, it found no link either way rather than a protective one.
The absence of a link for grandiose narcissism also contrasts with research covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which tied both grandiose and vulnerable traits to brain differences connected to hiding one’s feelings. That difference may reflect what was measured: the brain study looked at the specific habit of suppressing outward emotional expressions, while the meta-analysis assessed broader difficulties managing emotions.
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Every study included in the meta-analysis relied on self-report questionnaires, which depend on participants being both honest and self-aware about their flaws. The authors point to a 2023 study that recorded facial muscle activity and found amplified emotional reactions to negative social evaluation among people with grandiose traits, suggesting questionnaires may miss some of their emotional responses.
“I also wouldn’t interpret the lack of a relationship with grandiose narcissism as definitive evidence that people high in grandiose narcissism don’t experience difficulties regulating their emotions,” Willis cautioned. “All of the studies relied on self-report measures, and people high in grandiose narcissism may be less likely to perceive or report difficulties with emotion regulation.”
All 26 studies also used cross-sectional designs, measuring personality and emotional habits at a single point in time. In addition, half of the studies (13 of 26) recruited only university students, and most were conducted in Western nations, meaning the findings may not apply equally to older adults or different cultural contexts.
“The main caveat is that all of the studies included in our meta-analysis were cross-sectional, so we can’t determine the direction of the relationship,” Willis said. “Difficulties regulating emotions may contribute to the development or maintenance of vulnerable narcissism, vulnerable narcissism may contribute to difficulties regulating emotions, or other factors may explain this relationship.”
One such shared factor the authors raise is early experience: vulnerable narcissism has been theorized to arise partly from childhood trauma or inconsistent parenting, which may also hinder the development of emotional skills. Results also varied widely from study to study, so the pooled correlations are best read as averages rather than as figures that apply equally to every group or questionnaire. Several statistical checks did suggest the findings were unlikely to be skewed by publication bias, the tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often.
Another limitation is that too few studies reported detailed breakdowns of the six emotional problem areas to allow the authors to test grandiose and vulnerable narcissism separately for each specific skill. The authors recommend that future studies routinely report data for all individual emotion regulation subscales alongside total scores, use longitudinal designs that follow people over time, and recruit more diverse samples across cultures and age groups. Even with these limitations, the authors suggest that therapies focused on emotion regulation, such as dialectical behavior therapy or schema therapy, may be worth testing for people high in vulnerable narcissism, though studies have yet to show whether such treatment improves their well-being or relationships.
Looking ahead, the research team is now examining the roots of these traits and how emotional habits take shape over time. In psychology, insecure attachment refers to relationship patterns characterized by anxiety or avoidance that often stem from inconsistent caregiving early in life.
“One of the things I’m particularly interested in now is understanding how vulnerable narcissism may develop,” Willis told PsyPost. “We’re currently testing models looking at the potential role of insecure attachment and difficulties identifying, understanding and regulating emotions. Ultimately, we want to identify potentially modifiable factors that could be targeted through prevention or intervention strategies.”
The study, “The relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation: A systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Ria Tziliaskopoulos, Rose Ferguson, Wendy Song, and Megan L. Willis.

articles.title: ‘Prioritise welfare over military directives’: India raps Pak on minority rights at UN
articles.body:
New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India.
NEW DELHI: India tore into Pakistan at the United Nations for exploiting the international forum to spread propaganda while failing to protect its own citizens. New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India and demanded that Pakistan vacate all territories under its illegal occupation.Speaking at an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues at the UN General Assembly's Third Committee, India's First Secretary at the Permanent Mission to the UN, Raghoo Puri, called out Pakistan's conduct and said its representatives should focus on the welfare of their own people instead of taking directions from the military."Pakistan predictably misused the forum for propaganda. Jammu & Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India. Pakistan must vacate the territory under its illegal occupation," Puri said.He further said Pakistani representatives would do well to look inwards and address the concerns of their own citizens rather than act on military directives.
India slams Pakistan over minority rights
Puri underlined that protecting minority rights was primarily the sovereign responsibility of individual states, guided by the principle of sovereign equality.He said India's civilisational tradition of diversity was reflected in its constitutional safeguards for religious and linguistic minorities.
He also highlighted the substantial contributions made by minorities to India's national development, including at the highest levels of government and key institutions.
The latest confrontation followed India's strong rebuke to Pakistan at the UN on October 23 over its treatment of religious minorities. New Delhi accused Islamabad of failing to protect vulnerable communities while attempting to lecture India on religious freedom, burial rights and minority protections.During an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief, India's First Secretary at the UN mission, Bhavika Mangalanandan, challenged the report's approach to religious discrimination during the Covid-19 pandemic and its advocacy concerning funeral rights for terrorists.Mangalanandan argued that the report appeared to place disproportionate emphasis on discriminatory practices and shortcomings in countries in the Global South while overlooking similar tragedies in developed nations.
India asserts climate justice and judicial independence
Separately, India also defended its approach to climate change at the UN General Assembly, stressing the importance of equity, climate justice and sustainable development.Deputy secretary Barkha Tamrakar delivered India's statement before the Third Committee on the report of the Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, titled “An urgent and existential threat: the role of justice systems in addressing the climate crisis.”Tamrakar described climate change as a serious global challenge with consequences for development, livelihoods and human rights. She said India's response was guided by equity, climate justice, sustainable development and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC).
She highlighted the Constitution, environmental legislation, the National Green Tribunal and an independent judiciary as key safeguards supporting environmental protection in India.Tamrakar also noted that the Supreme Court had recognised the fundamental rights to life and equality as essential protections against the adverse effects of climate change.On judicial independence, she pointed to transparent, institutionally supervised training programmes, including those conducted by the National Judicial Academy, as measures to strengthen impartiality and safeguard the independence of the judiciary.
